title: A*
summary: A* orders frontier paths by f=g+h: cost already paid plus a lower estimate of remaining cost. An admissible h never exceeds the true cheapest remaining cost. With appropriate repeated-state handling, this lower bound prevents a more expensive goal from beating every frontier path that could lead to an optimal one. Consistency is the stronger edge-local condition that permits finalizing a state on its first minimum-f removal.
outcomes: Explain admissibility, consistency and the role of reopening.
Trace why g+h leaves an expensive completion on the frontier.

sources.label: Berkeley CS188: A*, admissibility and graph-search reopening
Russell and Norvig: search, depth limits and repeated states

labs.title: Spend search effort where a cheap completion remains possible
labs.summary: Compare the bill so far plus the cheapest plausible finish.
labs.assumptions: The directed graph has S→A→C→D→G with unit edge costs, S→B with cost 1, and B→G with cost 9. Start S; goal G. Costs are credits; drawn distances carry no meaning. The fixed heuristic is h(S)=4, h(A)=3, h(B)=9, h(C)=2, h(D)=1, h(G)=0. It happens to equal exact remaining costs in this tiny demonstration; obtaining it is not free in a real problem. Strict g improvements update frontier paths. Equal f values use alphabetical labels.
labs.accessibilitySummary: A*. The directed graph has S→A→C→D→G with unit edge costs, S→B with cost 1, and B→G with cost 9. Start S; goal G. Costs are credits; drawn distances carry no meaning. The fixed heuristic is h(S)=4, h(A)=3, h(B)=9, h(C)=2, h(D)=1, h(G)=0. It happens to equal exact remaining costs in this tiny demonstration; obtaining it is not free in a real problem. Strict g improvements update frontier paths. Equal f values use alphabetical labels. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: A valid heuristic prioritizes lower bounds on complete solutions. This example avoids expanding B, but a useful real heuristic must balance accuracy, evaluation cost and memory.

title: AC-3
summary: AC-3 enforces binary arc consistency with a work queue. A revision deletes tail values that lack head-domain support. When that domain shrinks, neighboring arcs that depended on its values are scheduled again. On finite domains, deletions eventually stop; failure is detected if a domain becomes empty.
outcomes: Follow domain changes and requeued dependencies in AC-3.
Distinguish its fixed point from a solved CSP.

sources.label: Berkeley CS188: forward checking and arc filtering
Poole and Mackworth: consistency algorithms and their limits

labs.title: A deleted support sends an earlier arc back to the queue
labs.summary: A check that passed yesterday can lose its witness today.
labs.equation: REVISE(X,Y): remove x with no compatible y; if D(X) shrinks, enqueue Z→X for neighbors Z≠Y
labs.assumptions: A<B<C, each initial domain {1,2,3,4}. FIFO starts [A→B,B→A,B→C,C→B]. Queue entries are deduplicated; after revising X→Y, requeue other neighbors into X. One slider step is one completed revision, regardless of the number of support comparisons inside it.
labs.accessibilitySummary: AC-3. A<B<C, each initial domain {1,2,3,4}. FIFO starts [A→B,B→A,B→C,C→B]. Queue entries are deduplicated; after revising X→Y, requeue other neighbors into X. One slider step is one completed revision, regardless of the number of support comparisons inside it. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: The queue tracks dependencies between domain reductions. Rechecking an affected arc is necessary to reach a fixed point, even if that arc passed earlier.

title: Admissible heuristics
summary: An admissible heuristic h is a lower bound on the least remaining cost h* from each state to a goal. Under the usual nonnegative convention, 0≤h≤h* and h(goal)=0. The inequality is a property over all relevant states, not merely over the path a search happened to return. It supports A* optimality when repeated states are handled correctly.
outcomes: Distinguish admissibility from consistency and empirical success.
Derive valid heuristic combinations and recognize unsupported overestimates.

sources.label: Berkeley CS188: heuristic lower bounds and A*
Poole and Mackworth: informed search and relaxed problems

labs.title: Break the bound, then watch when the answer breaks
labs.summary: An overestimate removes a guarantee before it necessarily changes an answer.
labs.assumptions: S→A→C→D→G has four unit-cost edges. S→B costs 1; B→G costs 9. Start S, goal G. The exact optimum is 4 credits. Numeric edge labels define costs; drawing lengths do not. Only h(A) changes; all other heuristic values are zero. A* uses g+h and permits strict g improvements, including reopening. Equal priorities use alphabetical state labels. The exact-distance table is an oracle for this tiny authored example, not a free ingredient in general search.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Admissible heuristics. S→A→C→D→G has four unit-cost edges. S→B costs 1; B→G costs 9. Start S, goal G. The exact optimum is 4 credits. Numeric edge labels define costs; drawing lengths do not. Only h(A) changes; all other heuristic values are zero. A* uses g+h and permits strict g improvements, including reopening. Equal priorities use alphabetical state labels. The exact-distance table is an oracle for this tiny authored example, not a free ingredient in general search. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Admissibility is a sufficient global condition, not a test inferred from one successful run. A heuristic can be inadmissible yet happen to return the optimum on a particular instance.

title: Alpha-beta pruning
summary: Alpha-beta search computes the same root minimax value while skipping descendants that cannot improve the relevant decision. Alpha carries a maximizing alternative and beta a minimizing restriction along the search path. Once alpha is at least beta, continuing that branch cannot improve the ancestor's choice under the stated tie policy. A cutoff can return a bound rather than an exact interior value; those meanings must survive caching and display.
outcomes: Justify a cutoff from an available alternative and opposing bound.
Interpret an incomplete interior result without inventing an exact score.

sources.label: Berkeley CS188: minimax, alpha-beta and evaluation functions
Rasmussen: Parallel Chess Searching and Bitboards, §3.2

labs.title: A reply can refute a branch before its other leaf is read
labs.summary: You do not need an exact losing branch to keep a better alternative.
labs.equation: At MAX: α←max(α,v); at MIN: β←min(β,v); cutoff when α≥β
labs.assumptions: Use the same two-ply zero-sum tree as Minimax: A leaves 3,5; B leaves b1,9. Search A before B and each branch's left leaf before its right. Start the root with (−∞,+∞). Fail-soft returns the best value seen, retaining bound status on an incomplete branch. Equality cuts off; first-child ties are retained. The four-leaf reference calculation is separate from the algorithmic visit count.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Alpha-beta pruning. Use the same two-ply zero-sum tree as Minimax: A leaves 3,5; B leaves b1,9. Search A before B and each branch's left leaf before its right. Start the root with (−∞,+∞). Fail-soft returns the best value seen, retaining bound status on an incomplete branch. Equality cuts off; first-child ties are retained. The four-leaf reference calculation is separate from the algorithmic visit count. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: A establishes α=3. At b1=2, B supplies an upper bound of 2, so b2 is pruned. At b1=4, that refutation is unavailable and all four terminals must be evaluated.

title: Arc consistency
summary: A directed binary arc X→Y is consistent when every value in the current domain of X has at least one compatible value in the current domain of Y. A network is arc consistent when every such arc passes. Supports can differ from edge to edge; they need not assemble into a complete solution.
outcomes: Check directed support and distinguish it from a global assignment.
Construct an arc-consistent unsatisfiable network.

sources.label: Poole and Mackworth: consistency algorithms and their limits
Berkeley CS188: forward checking and arc filtering

labs.title: Every edge has support; the triangle still cannot close
labs.summary: Separate witnesses are not a shared witness.
labs.equation: ∀x ∈ D(X), ∃y ∈ D(Y): cXY(x,y); check both directions for each binary relation
labs.assumptions: Triangle A,B,C has A≠B, B≠C, A≠C and equal input domains {1,…,q}. The slider chooses q=1,2,3. The lab checks support in these input domains; it does not run a pruning queue. Complete solution counts are exhaustive enumeration.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Arc consistency. Triangle A,B,C has A≠B, B≠C, A≠C and equal input domains {1,…,q}. The slider chooses q=1,2,3. The lab checks support in these input domains; it does not run a pruning queue. Complete solution counts are exhaustive enumeration. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: The two-color triangle is arc consistent and unsatisfiable. Arc consistency can exclude unsupported values without deciding arbitrary cyclic CSPs.

title: Backtracking
summary: Backtracking explores partial assignments depth first. It tries a value, checks constraints whose inputs are available, and either extends the prefix or undoes the choice. Finite domains and exhaustive alternatives make the basic procedure complete. Variable order, filtering and value order determine how much of the tree it visits.
outcomes: Trace extension, rejection and restoration of partial assignments.
Explain why a finite exhaustive backtracking run is complete.

sources.label: Poole and Mackworth: search over partial assignments

labs.title: Reject a bad prefix before filling the remaining slots
labs.summary: A failed prefix poisons every completion below it.
labs.equation: if a partial assignment violates a hard constraint, prune all of its extensions
labs.assumptions: Domains are {1,2,3}, constraints A<B and B<C, variable order A then B then C, and ascending values. Check the new adjacent inequality immediately. The run enumerates all solutions rather than stopping at the first. One attempt means trying a single variable value; it is not a complete-assignment test or a processor instruction.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Backtracking. Domains are {1,2,3}, constraints A<B and B<C, variable order A then B then C, and ascending values. Check the new adjacent inequality immediately. The run enumerates all solutions rather than stopping at the first. One attempt means trying a single variable value; it is not a complete-assignment test or a processor instruction. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Checking constraints early saves work, but undoing branch state is equally essential: a sibling must not inherit a failed branch's assignments or deletions.

title: Backward chaining
summary: Backward chaining starts with a query and replaces a selected goal with the body of a rule having that goal as its head. A fact discharges a goal; a conjunctive body requires every subgoal, while alternative defining rules provide different proof routes. Search order, cycles and repeated subgoals affect execution. A complete failed search can establish non-entailment in its stated finite setting, but that does not automatically prove a classical negation.
outcomes: Expand a query into its conjunctive evidence requirements.
Interpret a complete failed proof without inventing a negative conclusion.

sources.label: Poole and Mackworth: definite clauses, bottom-up and top-down proofs
CMU Automated Theorem Proving: Horn logic and chaining

labs.title: Ask only for the evidence needed to prove D
labs.summary: Follow the requested conclusion back to its evidence.
labs.equation: To prove head(r), prove every atom in body(r); alternative rules are alternative proof routes
labs.assumptions: Query D. Rules are A∧B⇒D, P⇒A, Q⇒B, plus irrelevant C⇒C. The mask supplies facts P and/or Q. Use left-to-right depth-first subgoals, stop a conjunction at its first failure, and check ancestor cycles. The query's actual dependency graph is acyclic with one defining rule per non-fact; the lab neither assumes missing facts false nor executes negation-as-failure.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Backward chaining. Query D. Rules are A∧B⇒D, P⇒A, Q⇒B, plus irrelevant C⇒C. The mask supplies facts P and/or Q. Use left-to-right depth-first subgoals, stop a conjunction at its first failure, and check ancestor cycles. The query's actual dependency graph is acyclic with one defining rule per non-fact; the lab neither assumes missing facts false nor executes negation-as-failure. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: With only P, A is proved but Q cannot discharge B, so D is not entailed. Supplying P and Q proves both branches and D. The unrelated C cycle is never entered.

title: Beam search
summary: Beam search keeps only a limited number of promising candidates. This lesson uses a level-synchronous variant: generate the next layer, merge duplicate states, rank candidates and retain at most k. The width controls retained alternatives, but permanently discarded paths can contain the only solution or the optimum. A valid heuristic alone cannot recover an erased branch.
outcomes: Explain why width pruning can lose completeness and optimality.
Reproduce a beam run from its score, merge, truncation and goal policies.

sources.label: Lemons et al. (2022): beam-search variants and non-monotonic width behavior
University of Pittsburgh: heuristic search and beam truncation

labs.title: What disappears when the beam narrows?
labs.summary: A beam is a shortlist, not a proof that everything outside it is worse.
labs.equation: B_next = first k candidates ranked by (h, alphabetical state)
labs.assumptions: S→A,B,C each costs 1; A→D costs 1 and D is a dead end; B→G costs 8; C→G costs 1. h(C)=1 and all other h=0. Generate a complete next layer; merge the same state by lowest g; rank by h then alphabetically; retain k; accept a retained goal. Discarded candidates are never revisited. This h-ranked layer beam is not the f-ranked variant in every reference.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Beam search. S→A,B,C each costs 1; A→D costs 1 and D is a dead end; B→G costs 8; C→G costs 1. h(C)=1 and all other h=0. Generate a complete next layer; merge the same state by lowest g; rank by h then alphabetically; retain k; accept a retained goal. Discarded candidates are never revisited. This h-ranked layer beam is not the f-ranked variant in every reference. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Beam width limits alternatives, not solution quality. Failure after pruning does not prove the original problem infeasible, and a surviving goal need not be cheapest.

title: Bidirectional search
summary: Bidirectional search grows one search from the start and another from the goal. A meeting joins a forward prefix to a valid suffix, potentially reducing the depth explored on either side. Correctness depends on the reverse transition relation, each side's search order and a justified stopping rule—not merely on drawing two arrows toward one another.
outcomes: Reconstruct a valid route from forward and backward distance maps.
Identify when reverse branching or a stopping rule defeats the expected saving.

sources.label: Poole and Mackworth: forward, backward and bidirectional search
Russell and Norvig: bidirectional search and problem formulation

labs.title: Two distance maps meet in the middle
labs.summary: Backward search asks who could reach this state, not where this state can go.
labs.equation: candidate length through v = d_forward(v) + d_backward(v)
labs.assumptions: Finite directed unit-cost graph: S→A,B; A→C,D; B→E,F; C→G; F→G. Alternate complete BFS layers, forward first. The backward side enumerates predecessors in the original graph. Mark on discovery within each side. After completing a layer, choose the shortest intersection; alphabetical ties choose C over F. This is unit-cost bidirectional BFS, not bidirectional Dijkstra or A*.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Bidirectional search. Finite directed unit-cost graph: S→A,B; A→C,D; B→E,F; C→G; F→G. Alternate complete BFS layers, forward first. The backward side enumerates predecessors in the original graph. Mark on discovery within each side. After completing a layer, choose the shortest intersection; alphabetical ties choose C over F. This is unit-cost bidirectional BFS, not bidirectional Dijkstra or A*. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: The two maps measure different directions. Meeting is useful only when the reverse transitions and stopping argument preserve a valid shortest route.

title: Boolean satisfiability
summary: Boolean satisfiability asks whether at least one complete truth assignment makes a formula true. In conjunctive normal form, every clause must hold, while each clause needs only one true literal. A SAT witness can be checked by evaluating the original formula. A failed trial proves only that trial invalid; UNSAT requires excluding all assignments through a complete procedure or a checkable refutation.
outcomes: Check every clause of a Boolean witness.
Explain why an invalid candidate is not an infeasibility proof.

sources.label: Berkeley CS188: entailment, enumeration and DPLL
Stanford Logic Programming: constraint search and unit propagation

labs.title: Two configurations survive three Boolean requirements
labs.summary: OR gives a clause alternatives; AND makes every clause compulsory.
labs.assumptions: X enables a fast mode, Y enables a safe mode and Z enables a cache. Require at least one mode, fast implies cache, and safe excludes cache. The eight assignments are exhaustive for exactly these three Boolean variables; no optimization score or omitted operational requirement is part of this model.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Boolean satisfiability. X enables a fast mode, Y enables a safe mode and Z enables a cache. Require at least one mode, fast implies cache, and safe excludes cache. The eight assignments are exhaustive for exactly these three Boolean variables; no optimization score or omitted operational requirement is part of this model. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: 010 and 101 satisfy all clauses. Selecting 111 violates the safe/cache exclusion even though the other two clauses hold. A failed selection does not negate the existing witnesses.

title: Branch and bound
summary: Branch and bound searches partial decisions while comparing each region's optimistic bound with the best complete feasible answer already known. For maximization, an upper bound that cannot exceed the incumbent makes a branch unnecessary when only one optimum is required. The method is exact when branching covers all possibilities and every prune is justified, but its worst-case search can remain exponential.
outcomes: Distinguish a feasible incumbent from an optimistic relaxation.
Choose the correct pruning inequality and explain its assumptions.

sources.label: MIT 1.204: branch and bound with fractional knapsack bounds
Poole and Mackworth: depth-first branch and bound for cost minimization

labs.title: A feasible packing competes with an impossible promise
labs.summary: A promise may beat your answer; an answer must obey every constraint.
labs.assumptions: Three whole items A,B,C with weights (4,3,2), profits (7,5,3), capacity 5. Branch include-first in A,B,C order, already sorted by profit/weight. At each feasible prefix, excluding all remaining items supplies a feasible completion. Compute an upper bound by filling remaining capacity fractionally with undecided items. Prune U≤incumbent; reject overweight prefixes separately. Seed choices are 000,001,010,100,011. Find one optimum, not all ties.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Branch and bound. Three whole items A,B,C with weights (4,3,2), profits (7,5,3), capacity 5. Branch include-first in A,B,C order, already sorted by profit/weight. At each feasible prefix, excluding all remaining items supplies a feasible completion. Compute an upper bound by filling remaining capacity fractionally with undecided items. Prune U≤incumbent; reject overweight prefixes separately. Seed choices are 000,001,010,100,011. Find one optimum, not all ties. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: The incumbent is attainable; the relaxation is optimistic. Pruning is a comparison between those two different certificates, with the inequality reversed for minimization.

title: Breadth-first search
summary: Breadth-first search explores paths in nondecreasing edge count using a FIFO frontier. In a graph implementation, recording a state when it is first enqueued prevents duplicate work and preserves a shortest unweighted path to it. This is a guarantee about depth; minimum monetary, energy or travel cost requires equal positive edge costs or a different search policy.
outcomes: Derive the shortest-edge guarantee from FIFO order.
Recognize when a weighted objective requires uniform-cost search instead.

sources.label: Berkeley CS188: frontier policies and uninformed search
Russell and Norvig: search, depth limits and repeated states

labs.title: The shallow answer can be expensive
labs.summary: A two-stop route can cost more than four cheap steps.
labs.equation: depth(child)=depth(parent)+1; enqueue at the back, remove from the front
labs.assumptions: The directed graph has S→A→C→D→G with unit edge costs, S→B with cost 1, and B→G with cost 9. Start S; goal G. Costs are credits; drawn distances carry no meaning. Successors are ordered alphabetically. A state is enqueued only on first discovery. The goal test occurs on removal, before generating successors. The slider counts removals, including the goal. Dashed coral follows the last removed node's path.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Breadth-first search. The directed graph has S→A→C→D→G with unit edge costs, S→B with cost 1, and B→G with cost 9. Start S; goal G. Costs are credits; drawn distances carry no meaning. Successors are ordered alphabetically. A state is enqueued only on first discovery. The goal test occurs on removal, before generating successors. The slider counts removals, including the goal. Dashed coral follows the last removed node's path. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: BFS certifies fewest edges, not lowest arbitrary cost. Its frontier order is the proof: no deeper path can jump ahead of a shallower one.

title: Classical Artificial Intelligence
summary: Classical AI represents a problem with explicit states, rules, constraints and objectives, then reasons or searches for a result. Its useful question is not just whether an answer looks plausible, but whether it satisfies the model and what guarantees the procedure provides. Search, logic, constraint solving, planning and game reasoning offer different tools for different structures.
outcomes: Separate model, solver, feasible answer and optimality certificate.
Choose a classical-AI learning path from the structure and guarantees of the task.

sources.label: Berkeley CS188: variables, domains and constraint satisfaction
Google OR-Tools: scheduling precedence, non-overlap and makespan
Berkeley CS188: search states and problem formulation

labs.title: Three tasks, explicit rules, one checkable plan
labs.summary: Adding a worker helps until the dependency—not the workforce—becomes the bottleneck.
labs.equation: minimize max(s_A,s_B,s_C)+1; s_A+1≤s_C; s_B≠s_C; concurrent tasks≤workers
labs.assumptions: Three deterministic nonpreemptive unit-duration tasks A,B,C, each using one identical worker. Start times belong to {0,1,2}, measured from time zero. A must finish before C starts; B and C cannot overlap. Capacity is one to three workers. Enumerate all 27 assignments, retain feasible ones, minimize finish time, and break ties lexicographically by (s_A,s_B,s_C). No setup times, uncertain durations or worker-specific qualifications.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Classical Artificial Intelligence. Three deterministic nonpreemptive unit-duration tasks A,B,C, each using one identical worker. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Separate the representation, feasibility rules, objective, solving procedure and certificate. More resources cannot remove a dependency that the model makes mandatory.

title: Completeness
summary: A search procedure is complete for a stated problem class if it eventually finds a solution whenever one exists, assuming the required operations terminate and sufficient resources are available. This is not a deadline guarantee. Nor does it automatically require termination on every unsolvable infinite instance. A single solvable instance on which a procedure runs forever refutes completeness for a class containing that instance.
outcomes: State a completeness guarantee with its domain and termination assumptions.
Distinguish exhaustion, timeout and a proved infinite counterexample.

sources.label: Russell and Norvig: search guarantees and resource analysis
Berkeley CS188: uninformed search policies and guarantees

labs.title: A goal one step away can wait forever
labs.summary: Never revisiting a state does not guarantee that every branch gets a turn.
labs.equation: solution exists ⇒ search eventually returns a solution (under the stated assumptions)
labs.assumptions: S has successors A0 then G. For every nonnegative integer i, Ai has exactly one successor A(i+1). Only G is a goal. This is an infinite acyclic graph with finite branching and unit costs. Compare A-first DFS and FIFO BFS, both testing the goal on removal. The slider limits the displayed run; it does not truncate the mathematical graph or prove nontermination from a finite prefix.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Completeness. S has successors A0 then G. For every nonnegative integer i, Ai has exactly one successor A(i+1). Only G is a goal. This is an infinite acyclic graph with finite branching and unit costs. Compare A-first DFS and FIFO BFS, both testing the goal on removal. The slider limits the displayed run; it does not truncate the mathematical graph or prove nontermination from a finite prefix. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Completeness is a quantified guarantee with assumptions, not a success rate on examples. Distinct-state infinite branches can defeat DFS even when a goal is shallow.

title: Consistent heuristics
summary: A consistent heuristic satisfies h(u)≤c(u,v)+h(v) on every directed edge and has zero value at goals. The estimate cannot drop by more than the actual edge cost. This makes A*'s f values nondecreasing along each path and supports finalizing a state at its first minimum-f removal. Admissibility alone does not supply that stronger guarantee.
outcomes: Relate edge consistency to nonnegative reduced costs.
Explain and trace reopening under an admissible inconsistent heuristic.

sources.label: Poole and Mackworth: consistency and multiple-path pruning

title: Constraint propagation
summary: Constraint propagation repeatedly narrows domains using deductions justified by relations and current domains. A sound propagator preserves every solution compatible with the current branch. title: Constraint-satisfaction problems
summary: A constraint-satisfaction problem specifies variables, a domain for each variable, and relations that permitted assignments must satisfy. A solution assigns every variable a domain value and satisfies all hard constraints. title: Depth-first search
summary: Depth-first search prioritizes continuing the current branch before returning to alternatives. A stack or recursive call chain encodes this policy. It is useful for reachability and structural graph algorithms, but the first goal found does not in general minimize either depth or cost. Termination and memory claims depend on how repeated states are handled.

Qualify DFS completeness and memory bounds for the actual implementation.

States are marked on discovery. Goal testing is on removal.

title: Depth-limited search

title: Dijkstra's algorithm
summary: Dijkstra's algorithm computes shortest distances from one source in a graph with nonnegative edge weights. It repeatedly finalizes the unsettled vertex with minimum tentative distance and relaxes its outgoing edges. The nonnegative assumption makes that finalization safe. The distance table is a result for every reachable vertex, not just one selected goal.
outcomes: Explain why nonnegative edges permit permanent distance finalization.

labs.assumptions: Directed edges are S→A=4, S→B=0, B→A=2, A→C=1 and B→C=5. U is isolated. Initialize d(S)=0 and other labels to infinity. title: DPLL
summary: DPLL is a complete backtracking procedure for finite propositional CNF. It simplifies clauses under a partial assignment, propagates forced unit literals, and branches on an unassigned variable when needed. A false clause closes that branch; all satisfied clauses permit a witness completion. Chronological backtracking restores the previous decision context before trying the opposite value. Completeness does not imply a practical worst-case time bound.
outcomes: Distinguish a decision, a forced propagation and a branch conflict.
Restore a failed branch and complete a satisfying partial trail.

labs.summary: Do not branch on a choice that a unit clause already forces.

labs.assumptions: CNF is C1=¬P∨Q, C2=¬P∨¬Q, C3=P∨R, C4=¬R∨S, C5=R∨¬S. Use alphabetic decisions, true first, first-clause unit propagation and chronological backtracking. This complete DPLL variant omits optional pure-literal elimination and clause learning. It stops when every original clause is satisfied, allowing remaining variables to be assigned either value.

title: Duplicate-state detection
summary: Duplicate-state detection recognizes when different search paths reach an equivalent state. Current-path cycle checking removes loops within one branch; a global reached table can also merge converging branches. The correct record is algorithm-dependent: a Boolean set can be enough for unweighted reachability, while cost or depth-limited search may need best-cost or remaining-budget information.

title: Expectimax
summary: Expectimax maximizes at controllable decisions and takes a probability-weighted expectation at chance nodes. It optimizes expected utility under the supplied transition or opponent model, rather than treating every uncontrolled choice as a worst-case adversarial reply. Probabilities must represent the actual conditional process, and leaf values must be utilities whose magnitudes support averaging. The best expectation is neither a guaranteed realized outcome nor robust to an incorrect probability model.
outcomes: Compute and compare a probability-weighted action value.
Separate expected-utility choice from worst-case guarantees and realized outcomes.

labs.assumptions: R chooses A or B. A has utility 0 with probability 1−p and utility 10 with probability p; B terminates at utility 4 for certain. The probabilities are supplied and sum to one; utilities are already on an expected-utility scale. This one-decision tree has no hidden observations, learning, capacity constraints or Monte Carlo sampling. First action A wins an exact tie.

title: First-order predicate logic
summary: First-order predicate logic describes objects, their properties and relations, and quantified statements about a domain. Constants name objects, variables range over them, predicates evaluate tuples, and function symbols denote domain-valued functions. Evaluating a sentence in one specified interpretation is different from showing it follows in every model of a knowledge base.

Regression planning instead searches over partial goal requirements: choose a relevant final action, ensure it does not delete a required fact, and replace the facts it achieves with its preconditions while retaining the other requirements. The resulting predecessor description is a condition on possible worlds, not one fully specified world or an inverse physical action. Both directions need search control and a correct action model.

title: Forward chaining
summary: Forward chaining starts with asserted facts and derives a rule's head when every body atom is known. For finite propositional definite clauses, repeated sound application reaches the least consequence closure. No additional applicable rule can enlarge that fixed point. title: Hill climbing
summary: Hill climbing improves a complete configuration by moving to a better neighbor according to an objective. Strict steepest ascent selects the highest-valued neighbor and stops if none improves the current value. Its stopping condition establishes a local maximum under the chosen neighborhood, rather than a global optimum over the full configuration space.
outcomes: Trace strict steepest ascent under a finite neighborhood.
Distinguish a local stopping condition from a global certificate.

sources.label: Berkeley CS188: local neighborhoods, hill climbing and beams
Poole and Mackworth: local search, restarts and memory

labs.title: A locally highest point can still leave three points behind
labs.summary: The neighborhood determines what uphill means.
labs.equation: xnext = argmaxy∈N(x) U(y); move only if U(xnext)>U(x)
labs.assumptions: Nine discrete configurations x=0,…,8 have utilities [1,4,7,6,3,5,8,10,9]. Neighbors are valid x±1. Use strict improvement and smaller-index ties. The graph joins discrete values for readability; intermediate positions are not available configurations. The full enumeration supplies the global benchmark.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Hill climbing. Nine discrete configurations x=0,…,8 have utilities [1,4,7,6,3,5,8,10,9]. Neighbors are valid x±1. Use strict improvement and smaller-index ties. The graph joins discrete values for readability; intermediate positions are not available configurations. The full enumeration supplies the global benchmark. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Five starting configurations end at utility seven; four end at utility ten. A strict local stop cannot certify which peak is globally best without additional information.

title: Horn clauses
summary: A Horn clause is a disjunction with at most one positive literal. A definite clause has exactly one: ¬A∨¬B∨C can be read as A∧B⇒C. A clause with no positive literal forbids its corresponding positive conjunction, while a positive unit clause is a fact. This syntactic restriction enables specialized propositional inference; it does not make arbitrary first-order programs terminate or make a rule into a causal assertion.
outcomes: Classify a clause by its positive-literal count.
Translate a definite clause without losing its joint antecedents.

sources.label: Poole and Mackworth: definite clauses, bottom-up and top-down proofs

labs.title: One positive head gives a conjunction a direction
labs.summary: Count the positive literals before treating a clause as a rule.
labs.assumptions: Classify five independent propositional clause examples: ¬A∨¬B∨C, ¬A∨B, ¬A∨¬B, A∨B and C. They are not asserted together as one KB. The diagram shows equivalent syntax, not a truth assignment. Positive means unnegated, not currently true. ⊥ denotes false.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Horn clauses. Classify five independent propositional clause examples: ¬A∨¬B∨C, ¬A∨B, ¬A∨¬B, A∨B and C. They are not asserted together as one KB. The diagram shows equivalent syntax, not a truth assignment. Positive means unnegated, not currently true. ⊥ denotes false. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: ¬A∨¬B∨C has one positive head C, but A∨B has two and is not Horn. ¬A∨¬B is Horn with no head and forbids A and B from both being true.

title: Iterative deepening
summary: Iterative deepening runs fresh depth-limited searches at limits zero, one, two and onward. Each run discards its search frontier; the outer loop continues only after a cutoff. With finite branching and a reachable finite-depth goal, the first successful limit equals the shallowest solution depth. This buys small depth-first working memory by repeating earlier work.
outcomes: Derive shallowest-goal correctness from the sequence of depth limits.
Assess repeated-work overhead separately from working-memory savings.

sources.label: Russell and Norvig: search, depth limits and repeated states
AIMA reference code: recursive depth-limited and iterative-deepening search

labs.title: Revisit the top to avoid storing the width
labs.summary: Explore one floor deeper, then start again with a smaller backpack.
labs.equation: for L=0,1,…: run DLS(L); continue only on cutoff
labs.assumptions: The directed graph has S→A→C→D→G with unit edge costs, S→B with cost 1, and B→G with cost 9. Start S; goal G. Costs are credits; drawn distances carry no meaning. Every run starts fresh, uses alphabetical DFS and current-path cycle checking, and tests goals before cutoffs. The control caps the outer loop. The process stops at its first success even if the selected cap is larger. Visit counts include boundary checks and repeated states across runs.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Iterative deepening. The directed graph has S→A→C→D→G with unit edge costs, S→B with cost 1, and B→G with cost 9. Start S; goal G. Costs are credits; drawn distances carry no meaning. Every run starts fresh, uses alphabetical DFS and current-path cycle checking, and tests goals before cutoffs. The control caps the outer loop. The process stops at its first success even if the selected cap is larger. Visit counts include boundary checks and repeated states across runs. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Iterative deepening finds a shallowest goal with depth-first working memory, but not a cheapest goal when costs differ. Repeated visits are a deliberate memory tradeoff.

title: Iterative deepening A*
summary: Iterative deepening A* (IDA*) runs depth-first passes bounded by f=g+h. It starts at h(start) and, after an unsuccessful pass, raises the threshold to the smallest f that exceeded the old bound. It preserves an admissible heuristic's cost guarantee under suitable termination conditions while trading A*'s stored frontier for repeated depth-first work.
outcomes: Compute the next IDA* threshold from exceeded f values.
Explain cost optimality and repeated-work tradeoffs without confusing IDA* with depth-only iteration.

sources.label: Korf (1985): original iterative-deepening and IDA* paper
Poole and Mackworth: background on admissible f bounds

labs.title: Raise a cost contour, not a depth limit
labs.summary: The next contour comes from the cheapest rejected possibility.
labs.equation: T₀=h(S); T_next=min{g(n)+h(n) : f(n)>T in this pass}
labs.assumptions: The graph is S→A→C→D→G with four unit-cost edges, S→B cost 1 and B→G cost 9. h equals half the exact remaining distance: S:2,A:1.5,B:4.5,C:1,D:0.5,G:0. Use alphabetical DFS, current-path cycle checking, and prune f>T before accepting a goal. Count all entered nodes, including cutoff and goal checks. Each pass restarts from S.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Iterative deepening A*. The graph is S→A→C→D→G with four unit-cost edges, S→B cost 1 and B→G cost 9. h equals half the exact remaining distance: S:2,A:1.5,B:4.5,C:1,D:0.5,G:0. Use alphabetical DFS, current-path cycle checking, and prune f>T before accepting a goal. Count all entered nodes, including cutoff and goal checks. Each pass restarts from S. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: IDA* deepens an f-cost bound, not an edge-depth bound. Taking the smallest exceeded score avoids skipping a potentially optimal cost contour; memory savings can come with substantial repeated work.

title: Least-constraining value
summary: Least-constraining value orders candidate values for a selected variable by their effect on the remaining variables. A common local score counts neighbor-domain values deleted by a trial assignment and filtering. Lower scores preserve more immediate alternatives. The score is a heuristic proxy, with ties and filtering strength defined by the implementation.
outcomes: Compute a local LCV score and expose a wipeout.
Distinguish a pruning proxy from a complete solution count.

sources.label: Berkeley CS188: variable and value ordering
Berkeley CS188: forward checking and arc filtering

labs.title: Try the value that leaves neighbors more choices
labs.summary: Choose your value without taking away someone else's last option.
labs.equation: score(x)=ΣY |D(Y) ∖ D(Y after trial X=x)|; prefer smaller score
labs.assumptions: X has {1,2,3}; neighbors Y={1,2}, Z={1,3}, W={1}. Relations are X≠Y,X≠Z,X≠W, with no relation among the neighbors. Score a trial using forward checking on a temporary copy. Ties use ascending numeric values. Full-extension counts are enumerated only to explain this independent-neighbor toy model.

labs.takeaway: X=1 empties W. X=2 and X=3 each remove only one neighbor value, so they tie; the declared rule chooses 2 first.

title: Local beam search
summary: Local beam search maintains a bounded population of complete configurations. It generates neighbors of every current member, pools the candidates, and chooses the next population using an objective. Selection is shared across members, so it differs from independent local searches. Deduplication, ties and whether parents are retained affect both diversity and behavior.
outcomes: Construct a next population from a shared successor pool.
Distinguish local populations, independent restarts and path-frontier beams.

sources.label: Berkeley CS188: local neighborhoods, hill climbing and beams

labs.title: Pool all neighbors before choosing the next population
labs.summary: One member's useful neighbor can become everyone's next direction.
labs.equation: Bnext = top-k unique configurations in ⋃x∈B N(x), ranked by utility
labs.assumptions: Three-bit configurations 000,…,111 have utilities [0,5,4,1,3,2,9,6] by numeric ID. A move flips one bit. Width k initializes with the first k members of [000,111,010]. Pool and deduplicate successors, then rank by decreasing utility and increasing ID. Parents are not automatically retained. Run at most three generations, stopping if known target 110 appears.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Local beam search. Three-bit configurations 000,…,111 have utilities [0,5,4,1,3,2,9,6] by numeric ID. A move flips one bit. Width k initializes with the first k members of [000,111,010]. Pool and deduplicate successors, then rank by decreasing utility and increasing ID. Parents are not automatically retained. Run at most three generations, stopping if known target 110 appears. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Width two pools the neighbors of 000 and 111 and discovers 110 immediately. Width one follows a different supplied initialization and misses it within three generations; this is a worked trace, not a monotonic width guarantee.

title: Min-conflicts
summary: Min-conflicts searches over complete assignments that may violate constraints. It selects a conflicted variable and replaces its value with one minimizing the conflicts involving that variable, holding all other values fixed. Repeated repair can quickly find feasible assignments on suitable problems, but local traps, cycles and budgets prevent a general completeness guarantee.
outcomes: Trace repair of a complete but inconsistent assignment.
Separate feasibility discovery from infeasibility or optimality certification.

sources.label: Berkeley CS188: repair of complete assignments
Poole and Mackworth: local search, restarts and memory

labs.title: Three clashes disappear after two color repairs
labs.summary: Keep every slot filled, then repair the clashes.
labs.equation: choose conflicted X; xnext = argminv∈D(X) number of violated constraints involving X
labs.assumptions: Triangle A,B,C uses colors {1,2,3} with pairwise inequality edges. Start (1,1,1). Select the alphabetically first conflicted variable and the smallest color among equal minima, including its current value as a candidate. The deterministic trace performs up to two repairs and stops at zero conflicts. It is one explicit policy, rather than a random performance experiment.

labs.takeaway: Repair A to 2, then B to 3, reducing edge conflicts 3→1→0. Zero means every modeled hard inequality is satisfied, not that an unrelated quality objective is optimized.

title: Minimax
summary: Minimax backs up terminal utilities through a finite game tree: maximize at your decisions and minimize at the opponent's decisions, keeping one fixed payoff perspective. In a two-player zero-sum perfect-information game, exhaustive search computes the value against optimal opposition. It also gives a worst-case guarantee against legal replies in that model. A shallow tree with heuristic leaf evaluations instead solves an approximation, not necessarily the original game.
outcomes: Back up a game tree in one fixed payoff perspective.
Distinguish a forceable value from the largest reachable payoff.

sources.label: Berkeley CS188: minimax, alpha-beta and evaluation functions
Rasmussen: Parallel Chess Searching and Bitboards, §3.2

labs.title: A tempting nine is not a payoff you can force
labs.summary: Judge a move by the reply your opponent would choose.
labs.assumptions: R belongs to MAX; its children A and B belong to MIN. A ends at payoffs 3 or 5; B ends at b1 or 9. The slider supplies b1 in utility points for MAX. MIN's payoff is the negative of MAX's. Two plies, four genuine terminals, no chance, hidden information, repeated states or cutoff estimates; left-to-right ties choose the first child.

title: Minimum remaining values
summary: Minimum remaining values selects an unassigned variable with the fewest currently legal choices. The score must reflect the current branch and its filtering, rather than the original declared domain. Ties need a policy, such as alphabetical order or residual degree. This ordering guides search; it is not a proof that the selected branch succeeds.
outcomes: Compute MRV from a current domain snapshot.
Distinguish variable selection from value selection.

labs.summary: Handle the slot closest to running out of options.
labs.equation: choose X ∈ unassigned minimizing |Dcurrent(X)|; an empty domain signals failure
labs.assumptions: Four unassigned variables have supplied current domains A={1,…,k}, B={1,2}, C={1,2,3}, D={1,2}. The slider varies k from one to three. Ties are alphabetical. This is an ordering snapshot: it does not assign a value, run filtering or measure full search work.

title: Monte Carlo tree search
summary: Monte Carlo tree search allocates a finite lookahead budget using statistics collected from completed simulations. This lab separates selection through an existing tree, expansion of one new child, a rollout through the domain and backup to the selected tree nodes. Inspect the exact trace and its changing estimates rather than treating a larger visit count as a proof. The example is single-agent optimization; it does not model an adversary or a learned neural evaluator.
outcomes: Trace selection, expansion, rollout and backup without conflating them.
Distinguish recorded estimates, simulation allocation and a final action recommendation.

sources.label: Browne et al.: A Survey of Monte Carlo Tree Search Methods, §3

labs.title: A rollout can see a leaf before the tree contains it
labs.summary: Search evidence grows one node at a time; a simulated state is not automatically a tree node.
labs.equation: N←N+1; W←W+r; Q=W/N; select Q+c√(ln Nparent/Nchild)
labs.assumptions: R chooses terminal A (reward 0.6) or decision B, which chooses L (0) or H (1). One agent controls both decisions; all rewards use the same [0,1] scale. Expand untried children left to right. Fully expanded nodes use UCT with c=√2 and first-child ties. Rollouts choose uniformly using a seed-7 32-bit generator. Backup touches selected/expanded tree nodes only. Recommend the most visited root child, A first on ties. The slider recomputes from the same seed, with no animation or background search.

labs.takeaway: Simulation 2 expands B and rolls out to L with reward 0, but L remains outside the search tree. Seeing a terminal in a rollout and maintaining its own visit statistics are different operations.

title: Negamax
summary: Negamax expresses zero-sum minimax with one maximization recurrence by measuring each position from its own side-to-move perspective. A child's score belongs to the opponent, so negate it before comparison at the parent. Under strictly alternating turns and opposite payoffs, this computes the same decision as fixed-perspective minimax. The simpler recurrence does not itself prune, sample or improve the evaluation function.
outcomes: Convert child scores into the parent's payoff perspective.
Explain why a symmetric recurrence is equivalent to minimax rather than a search-speed guarantee.

Terminal labels use the player who would move next. The slider changes which player owns R, so it changes the game, not merely a display perspective. title: Optimality
summary: A feasible result is optimal when its objective value is no worse than every other feasible result. An algorithmic optimality guarantee must hold over its stated problem class, not merely for one successful example. In path search, minimum edge count and minimum accumulated cost coincide only under suitable cost assumptions. A bound can quantify the gap when exact optimality has not been established.
outcomes: Distinguish instance optimality from an algorithm's universal guarantee.
Compute an additive gap and cost ratio without confusing cost with depth.

sources.label: Berkeley CS188: uninformed search policies and guarantees
Russell and Norvig: search guarantees and resource analysis

labs.title: Fewer edges stops meaning cheaper at one threshold
labs.summary: The shortest-looking route is only best after you name the cost.
labs.assumptions: Directed routes are S→B→G with edge costs 1,w and S→A→C→D→G with four unit costs. No other edges exist. w is nonnegative. BFS favors the two-edge route; DFS explores A before B; finite-graph UCS uses strict best-g updates and tests the goal on removal. The chart compares these fixed policies; it is not a benchmark over random graphs.

labs.takeaway: Optimality is relative to an objective and a feasible set. One counterexample defeats a universal claim, while one optimal run does not establish it.

title: Partial-order planning
summary: A partial-order plan contains action instances, ordering constraints and causal links that support requirements. A causal link says an earlier producer supplies a fact needed by a later consumer; a threatening action could delete that fact between them. Repairing the threat places it outside the protected interval or otherwise removes the conflict. A completed sound partial plan should permit only executable, goal-reaching linearizations under its action semantics, not merely include one successful total order.
outcomes: Identify a deleting threat to a causal link.
Explain two ordering repairs and why an unresolved plan is not safe merely because it has a valid execution.

sources.label: Poole and Mackworth: partial-order actions, causal support and threats
University of Washington: UCPOP partial-order planner

labs.title: Two valid orders do not make an unresolved partial plan safe
labs.summary: Protect the fact between the producer and its consumer.
labs.equation: Causal link P —r→ C requires P
labs.assumptions: Empty initial state. P has no preconditions and adds readiness r. C requires r and adds done d, preserving r. T has no preconditions, deletes r and adds audit flag a. Goal is d∧a. The audit flag records T's occurrence; it does not assert readiness remains false, so P may reestablish r later. All three instances are supplied, actions are sequential and instantaneous, and the control adds one threat-repair ordering. Enumerate and replay every compatible total order; this is a partial-plan checker, not a full planner.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Partial-order planning. Empty initial state. P has no preconditions and adds readiness r. C requires r and adds done d, preserving r. T has no preconditions, deletes r and adds audit flag a. Goal is d∧a. The audit flag records T's occurrence; it does not assert readiness remains false, so P may reestablish r later. All three instances are supplied, actions are sequential and instantaneous, and the control adds one threat-repair ordering. Enumerate and replay every compatible total order; this is a partial-plan checker, not a full planner. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: P<C alone permits P→C→T and T→P→C, but also failing P→T→C. Constraining T before P or after C protects readiness and leaves one valid order in this three-action example.

parameter.label: Threat repair: 0=none, 1=T before P, 2=T after C

title: PDDL
summary: PDDL separates a reusable action domain from a task instance containing objects, an initial state and a goal. Typed parameters define possible grounded bindings; preconditions determine which grounded actions are executable in a particular state. Declaring a language requirement expresses a needed feature, not a guarantee that a chosen planner supports it. A well-formed model can still describe the wrong world, and a valid plan need not optimize an undeclared objective.
outcomes: Separate action schemas, typed bindings and state-dependent applicability.
Read generated domain/problem text without confusing modeling with solver verification.

sources.label: Ghallab et al.: original PDDL manual, domains/actions/problems
Haslum: writing PDDL domains and problems

labs.title: One action schema becomes many bindings, but few legal moves
labs.summary: A parameter pair is only a candidate; the road and current location must both agree.
labs.equation: n locations ⇒ n² typed (?from,?to) bindings; applicable iff at(from)∧road(from,to)
labs.assumptions: Display an authored :strips :typing domain with one implicit traveler, predicates at(location) and road(location,location), and a move action deleting the old location and adding the new one. The generated instance has l0…l(n−1), bidirectional neighboring roads, initial (at l0), and final goal (at l(n−1)). No numeric metric or durations are declared. JavaScript enumerates the same semantics and uses unit-action BFS; it neither parses this PDDL nor calls an external planner.

The generated instance has l0…l(n−1), bidirectional neighboring roads, initial (at l0), and final goal (at l(n−1)). No numeric metric or durations are declared. JavaScript enumerates the same semantics and uses unit-action BFS; it neither parses this PDDL nor calls an external planner. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.

title: Propositional logic
summary: Propositional logic treats each atomic statement as Boolean and evaluates compound statements with truth-functional connectives. A truth assignment is a model of a formula when that formula evaluates to true. Syntax describes a formula; semantics tells which assignments satisfy it. Material implication is especially easy to misread: P⇒Q rules out P=true,Q=false, without asserting causation or the converse.
outcomes: Evaluate material implication and distinguish its converse.
Separate satisfaction of one model from validity across all models.

sources.label: Berkeley CS188: propositional models and CNF
Berkeley CS188: entailment, enumeration and DPLL

labs.title: An implication fails in just one of four worlds
labs.summary: Read an implication as one forbidden row, not an arrow of cause.
labs.assumptions: Use classical two-valued semantics with two independent proposition symbols P,Q. Assignment indices enumerate (P,Q)=00,01,10,11. The table compares the implication with its converse. No probability, causal direction, time ordering or real-world rule reliability is encoded.

The table compares the implication with its converse. No probability, causal direction, time ordering or real-world rule reliability is encoded. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: At P=0,Q=1, P⇒Q is true but Q⇒P is false. Three satisfying rows make P⇒Q satisfiable; its remaining false row prevents validity.

title: Quantifiers
summary: Universal quantification requires a formula for every domain element; existential quantification requires at least one witness. Nested quantifier order controls which witnesses may depend on earlier choices. ∀x∃y R(x,y) permits a different y for each x, whereas ∃y∀x R(x,y) requires one y that works for all x. Reversing these mixed quantifiers generally changes the claim.
outcomes: Compare dependent witnesses with one shared witness.
Negate a quantified statement and identify the correct counterexample.

sources.label: forall x: Calgary — multiple generality and quantifier order
Stanford Introduction to Logic: quantifier relationships and negation

labs.title: Every job can have a worker without sharing one worker
labs.summary: A one in every row is weaker than one column full of ones.
labs.equation: ∃w∈Workers ∀j∈Jobs R(j,w) ⇒ ∀j∈Jobs ∃w∈Workers R(j,w); converse is not valid
labs.assumptions: Jobs={j1,j2} and Workers={w1,w2,w3} are fixed nonempty finite sets. R(j,w) means that worker can handle that job. Four completely specified compatibility tables are supplied; the control changes the table, not the quantifier definition. Bounded quantifiers are shorthand for the stated typed restrictions. No worker capacity, distinctness or simultaneous assignment condition is encoded.

title: Random-restart hill climbing
summary: Random-restart hill climbing repeats local improvement from independently sampled initial configurations and keeps the best result. Its chance of success depends on the initialization distribution and the basins induced by the local policy. A finite number of runs still permits failure. Almost-sure eventual success requires a positive success probability and indefinitely many suitable trials.
outcomes: Calculate repeated-run success under explicit independence.
Explain the difference between finite-budget risk and eventual success.

labs.summary: Count basin probability, not the number of peaks.

labs.assumptions: Use the nine-state hill-climbing landscape and strict adjacent moves. Each run starts uniformly on 0,…,8, independently with replacement, and is allowed to finish. Four starts reach the global peak, so p=4/9. The plot is an exact probability calculation, not an empirical trial or runtime measurement.

title: Resolution
summary: Propositional resolution combines two clauses containing complementary literals on one pivot and keeps their other literals. The resulting clause follows from its parents. To prove that a knowledge base entails a query, add the negated query and seek the empty clause. A completed refutation establishes contradiction; an unfinished or arbitrarily truncated derivation cannot establish that no proof exists.
outcomes: Construct a resolvent from one complementary pivot pair.
Interpret an empty-clause refutation with the negated query included.

labs.title: A four-step refutation proves that C must hold
labs.summary: Make the denied conclusion impossible.
labs.equation: (A∨L),(B∨¬L) ⊢ A∨B; KB⊨q iff KB∧¬q is unsatisfiable
labs.assumptions: Use propositional clauses C1=A∨B, C2=¬A∨C, C3=¬B∨C. To prove C, add C4=¬C. The slider applies the four specified valid resolvents in order. Each step cancels exactly one complementary pair. A separate eight-assignment enumeration is labeled as an oracle, not counted as part of the resolution trace.

labs.takeaway: Negating C forces ¬A and ¬B, contradicting A∨B. The empty clause follows after four resolutions; KB alone remains consistent with three models.

title: Simulated annealing
summary: Simulated annealing proposes local moves and sometimes accepts a worse objective to escape a local trap. For minimization with the usual symmetric proposal rule, a cost increase ΔE is accepted with exp(−ΔE/T) at positive temperature. A cooling schedule changes these decisions over time. Convergence results require specific state-space, proposal and cooling assumptions; a finite practical run need not find a global optimum.
outcomes: Compute acceptance from a cost difference and temperature.
Separate a one-step decision from cooling-dependent convergence.

sources.label: Hajek: cooling schedules and asymptotic convergence
Poole and Mackworth: local search, restarts and memory

labs.title: Temperature sets the price of accepting a worse move
labs.summary: A controlled willingness to go uphill can open a route downhill.
labs.assumptions: Minimize E, use symmetric proposals and compare strictly worsening gaps 1,3,5 cost units. T has the same units as E, making ΔE/T dimensionless. T=0 is displayed as the limiting zero acceptance for positive gaps. This is a one-step probability lab, not a stochastic trajectory or an implemented cooling schedule.

A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: At T=1, a three-unit worsening proposal is accepted about 4.98% of the time. At T=3, it is accepted about 36.79%; proposal frequency and future cooling still matter.

title: State-space planning
summary: Classical state-space planning searches for an executable action sequence from a known initial world to any state satisfying a goal. Each action contributes a successor only where its preconditions hold. The state must retain all facts relevant to future legality and effects, not merely physical location. Goal satisfaction and plan quality are separate: a shortest-action plan is cheapest only when the declared action costs justify that objective.
outcomes: Construct legal planning successors from complete states.
Interpret an achievement goal and shortest-action result without inventing extra objectives.

sources.label: Poole and Mackworth: states, action representations and goals

labs.title: A location alone cannot tell you whether delivery is possible
labs.summary: The same office can contain an available, carried or delivered parcel state.
labs.equation: Applicable(a,s) iff pre(a)⊆s; successor=(s∖del(a))∪add(a); goal iff D∈s
labs.assumptions: H=robot at home, O=robot at office, P=parcel available at home, C=robot carrying it, D=parcel delivered. Positive state sets are complete closed-world descriptions. Pickup: pre H,P; delete P; add C. Go: pre H; delete H; add O. Back: pre O; delete O; add H. Deliver: pre O,C; delete C; add D. All other atom values persist. Sequential deterministic actions; no exogenous change or replenishment. Every action costs one. BFS uses action order Pickup, Go, Back, Deliver, marks complete states discovered on insertion and tests D on removal. The control chooses one of four reachable starts. Exhaustive reference reachability is computed separately from the original {H,P} start; it is not added to the early-stopping search count.

title: State-space representation
summary: A search state summarizes the past well enough to determine legal future actions, their outcomes and costs, and whether the goal is satisfied. It need not store the entire world or action history. But dropping a variable that changes the future can merge genuinely different situations and make an otherwise correct search algorithm return an invalid answer or miss a solution.
outcomes: Choose a state representation that preserves relevant future behavior.
Distinguish world state, search node, abstraction and reachable-state count.

labs.title: The hall before and after finding the key
labs.summary: Same room is not the same state when one arrival carries a key.
labs.assumptions: Three rooms: hall H, key room K and goal room G. H↔K is traversable; entering K automatically acquires a key that is never consumed. H→G requires the key; G is terminal. Every move costs one. Start in H with the selected key flag. Compare BFS using the full (room,key) state against the incorrect room-only duplicate key. K1↔H1 in the diagram is a two-way transition.

title: STRIPS
summary: In a propositional STRIPS model, an action has positive preconditions plus add and delete sets. If its preconditions are satisfied, remove the delete facts and insert the add facts; every other fact keeps its truth value. This compact persistence convention avoids listing an entire successor world for each action. It is a modeling assumption: omitted external changes, resources or conditional effects do not happen automatically just because the real system has them.
outcomes: Compute an add/delete successor while preserving untouched facts.
Distinguish action-list membership, state truth and rejected execution.

sources.label: Poole and Mackworth: states, action representations and goals

labs.title: Moving changes location, not the parcel in your hand
labs.summary: Delete, add, and leave the rest alone—but only after the gate opens.
labs.assumptions: H=robot at home, O=robot at office, P=parcel available at home, C=robot carrying it, D=parcel delivered. Positive state sets are complete closed-world descriptions. Pickup: pre H,P; delete P; add C. Go: pre H; delete H; add O. Back: pre O; delete O; add H. Deliver: pre O,C; delete C; add D. All other atom values persist. Sequential deterministic actions; no exogenous change or replenishment. The six cases inspect Pickup/Go/Deliver at explicit states, including rejected attempts. Preconditions, add and delete lists have positive-atom set representations with disjoint effects. No conditional effects, negative preconditions, derived predicates or continuous time are used. A rejected action has no after-state; it is not modeled as a legal no-op.

title: Tabu search
summary: Tabu search guides local moves with short-term memory that temporarily forbids specified moves, attributes or revisits. It can accept a worsening move when that move is the best admissible option. Aspiration criteria can override a restriction, often for an improvement over the best result seen. Memory definitions and tenure are part of the algorithm, and ordinary short-term tabu rules do not provide a universal optimality or no-cycle certificate.
outcomes: Trace state memory and temporary objective worsening.
Explain aspiration and the limits of finite tabu tenure.

labs.title: Remember the cheap return long enough to try the escape
labs.summary: A cheap return can be exactly the move that keeps you trapped.
labs.equation: choose the minimum-cost admissible neighbor; tabu override if E(new)<E(best seen)
labs.assumptions: Four states P,Q,R,G form an undirected chain with objective costs [0,1,4,−2]. Start P; choose the lowest-cost admissible neighbor. Memory stores the last t departed states and forbids reentry unless it beats the best cost seen. Stop at known target G or twelve moves. This state-memory variant differs from a move-attribute implementation. Aspiration is present but not triggered in this example.

labs.takeaway: At Q, excluding the immediate return P forces a visit to R at cost four, opening G at minus two. The best-so-far value must survive the temporary worsening.

title: Time and memory complexity
summary: Search resource analysis must name what is counted: generated nodes, removed entries, expanded states, frontier records, parent histories or duplicate tables. Branching and depth describe an implicit search tree; V and E describe an explicit finite graph. labs.title: The frontier grows exponentially; the depth-first stack does not
labs.summary: A small working stack can traverse a very large tree.
labs.equation: N=(3^(d+1)−1)/2; BFS frontier=3^d; eager DFS stack=1+2d
labs.assumptions: A complete ternary tree has root depth zero, three children per internal node, and leaves exactly at depth d. Traverse the entire bounded tree with no early goal stop and no duplicate states. BFS stores pending nodes in a FIFO queue. Eager DFS pops a node before pushing all three children; lazy DFS stores a successor iterator per active frame. Counts exclude parent histories, closed sets and the input graph. The illustrative byte conversion assumes 256 bytes per pending record, not measured JavaScript memory.

title: UCT
summary: UCT applies a bandit-style selection score within a Monte Carlo search tree. title: Early stopping
summary: Early stopping selects a training checkpoint using a validation metric and stops after a defined run of insufficient improvements.
outcomes: Simulate patience and identify the restored checkpoint.
Keep final test data outside checkpoint selection and stopping-rule tuning.

labs.title: Early stopping: calculate and compare
labs.summary: Keep the best checkpoint, not merely the checkpoint where patience runs out.
labs.equation: improvement: lossₜ < best_loss − min_delta; stop when wait ≥ patience
labs.assumptions: Illustrative fixed validation losses [0.90,0.70,0.55,0.50,0.51,0.52,0.49,0.53,0.54,0.55]. Lower is better, min_delta=0, one check per epoch, and the best observed checkpoint is restored.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Early stopping. Illustrative fixed validation losses [0.90,0.70,0.55,0.50,0.51,0.52,0.49,0.53,0.54,0.55]. Lower is better, min_delta=0, one check per epoch, and the best observed checkpoint is restored. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Patience changes which later improvements the run gets a chance to observe; the best available checkpoint can occur before the stopping epoch.
