labs.summary: The closest contour touches the line where no feasible tangent direction improves it.
labs.assumptions: An unconstrained-sign pair (x,y) in R² and one affine equality with nonzero normal (1,2). The contour is a circle centered at the origin; equal axis scales preserve its geometry. Only a finite segment of the infinite feasible line is displayed. All solutions and sensitivities are analytic.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Lagrange multipliers. An unconstrained-sign pair (x,y) in R² and one affine equality with nonzero normal (1,2). The contour is a circle centered at the origin; equal axis scales preserve its geometry. Only a finite segment of the infinite feasible line is displayed. All solutions and sensitivities are analytic. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Specify the Lagrangian's sign convention before interpreting its multiplier. Here dV/db=−λ, not λ.

title: Law of large numbers
summary: For i.i.d. integrable observations, the sample average converges to their common expectation. The weak law gives convergence in probability; the strong law gives almost-sure convergence. Neither says every successive sample average moves closer to the mean.
outcomes: Distinguish weak/strong convergence from monotonic improvement.
Calculate sample-mean variance under i.i.d. sampling.

sources.label: MIT 18.440: Probability and Random Variables — lecture notes

labs.title: The average concentrates
labs.summary: More observations narrow uncertainty; they do not force a smooth path.
labs.assumptions: The lab uses independent Bernoulli(0.3) observations. It plots the exact binomial distribution of their average, not one simulated sequence. The probability axis rescales to show the mass; the mean axis stays fixed.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Law of large numbers. The lab uses independent Bernoulli(0.3) observations. It plots the exact binomial distribution of their average, not one simulated sequence. The probability axis rescales to show the mass; the mean axis stays fixed. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Concentration of an average is different from the shape limit of its standardized error; the latter belongs to the CLT.

title: Law of total probability
summary: The law of total probability computes an event probability by splitting the sample space into disjoint, exhaustive cases and summing their joint contributions. Each conditional event rate is weighted by the probability of its case.
outcomes: Calculate a marginal probability from conditional rates.
Identify double counting and missing group weights.

sources.label: MIT 18.440: Probability and Random Variables — lecture notes

labs.title: Weight the branches before adding
labs.summary: A rare branch should not count as much as a common branch.
labs.assumptions: Groups A and B form a partition. The event rates are 0.1 in A and 0.7 in B. The bars show weighted contributions, not conditional rates. A zero-weight branch contributes zero.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Law of total probability. Groups A and B form a partition. The event rates are 0.1 in A and 0.7 in B. The bars show weighted contributions, not conditional rates. A zero-weight branch contributes zero. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Averaging group rates equally is correct only when the groups have equal probability.

title: Law of total variance
summary: For a random variable with finite second moment, total variance equals expected conditional variance plus the variance of the conditional mean. This identity separates residual variation within groups from variation attributable to differences between group means.
outcomes: Calculate within- and between-group variance.
Distinguish variance decomposition from causal explanation.

labs.title: Spread within groups plus spread between groups
labs.summary: Two tight groups can still make one widely spread population.
labs.assumptions: Two groups have probability 1/2 each. Their means are 0 and δ and both conditional variances are 1; a concrete construction is Y=δZ+ε with independent fair Z∈{0,1} and ε∈{−1,1}.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Law of total variance. Two groups have probability 1/2 each. Their means are 0 and δ and both conditional variances are 1; a concrete construction is Y=δZ+ε with independent fair Z∈{0,1} and ε∈{−1,1}. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: The decomposition is descriptive. Calling the between-group term an explained variance does not establish a causal explanation.

title: Learning rates and schedules
summary: A learning-rate schedule specifies how the optimizer's global step size changes with training progress. Its meaning depends on the clock—optimizer updates, examples, tokens, or epochs—and on the optimizer itself. Warmup and decay define a policy, not a general guarantee of better training.
outcomes: Translate warmup and cosine decay into explicit update values.
Distinguish a schedule policy from evidence that a model trained better.

sources.label: Loshchilov and Hutter: SGDR and cosine annealing

labs.title: Give the step size a clock
labs.summary: The schedule is a timetable; it does not measure whether the model has arrived.
labs.assumptions: The clock is the zero-based optimizer-update index. With W=0, warmup is skipped. Rates t=0…39 are applied; t=40 is the plotted zero endpoint, not another update. The last warmup update and first decay update both use the peak. Curves compare policies, not empirical training losses or warm restarts.

Curves compare policies, not empirical training losses or warm restarts. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: State the schedule's clock, endpoint convention, and warmup boundary. A visually smooth schedule can still be applied at the wrong frequency.

title: Limits and continuity
summary: A limit describes a function's behavior arbitrarily near an input, excluding the input itself. Continuity at that input additionally requires the assigned function value to agree with the limit. A function can have a perfectly well-defined limit while its value is missing or different.
outcomes: Distinguish a function value from a two-sided limit.
Use a matching condition to diagnose a removable discontinuity.

sources.label: OpenStax: the limit of a function

labs.title: Move one point without moving the limit
labs.summary: The neighbors determine the limit; the filled dot determines the value.
labs.equation: g(x)=x+1 for x≠1; g(1)=c; limₓ→₁ g(x)=2; continuity at 1 ⇔ c=2
labs.assumptions: A real piecewise function defined for every real x. An open circle marks the excluded point on the line when c≠2; a filled circle marks the actual value g(1). At c=2 the hole is filled. The graph shows a finite window, while the limit follows analytically from |g(x)−2|=|x−1| for x≠1.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Limits and continuity. A real piecewise function defined for every real x. An open circle marks the excluded point on the line when c≠2; a filled circle marks the actual value g(1). At c=2 the hole is filled. The graph shows a finite window, while the limit follows analytically from |g(x)−2|=|x−1| for x≠1. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Changing only the value at a point leaves its limit unchanged. Continuity asks whether those two independently specified quantities match.

title: Line search
summary: A line search chooses how far to move along an already chosen direction. It evaluates the one-dimensional restriction φ(α)=f(x+αp), looking for a useful step rather than necessarily solving that subproblem exactly. Direction selection, step acceptance and the outer optimizer's stopping rule are different decisions.
outcomes: Calculate an Armijo backtracking trace and its evaluation cost.
Distinguish step acceptance from direction choice and optimization termination.

sources.label: Boyd and Vandenberghe: descent methods and backtracking

labs.title: Reject the leap; accept enough progress
labs.summary: A direction is a heading, not permission to take an arbitrarily large step.
labs.assumptions: One line search on f(x)=2x² starts at x=1 with fixed direction p=−4. Use Armijo c₁=0.1 and halve rejected steps (ρ=0.5). Each slider setting restarts the search from its chosen initial trial; it is not an outer optimization iteration. Objective evaluations are deterministic, the direction is a descent direction, and all quantities are dimensionless. A small floating-point comparison tolerance handles equality at the acceptance boundary. Plot axes expand to include rejected trials.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Line search. One line search on f(x)=2x² starts at x=1 with fixed direction p=−4. Use Armijo c₁=0.1 and halve rejected steps (ρ=0.5). Each slider setting restarts the search from its chosen initial trial; it is not an outer optimization iteration. Objective evaluations are deterministic, the direction is a descent direction, and all quantities are dimensionless. A small floating-point comparison tolerance handles equality at the acceptance boundary. Plot axes expand to include rejected trials. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Sufficient decrease is an acceptance rule, not exact minimization or a certificate that the whole optimization problem is solved.

title: Linear algebra
summary: Linear algebra studies vector spaces and maps that preserve linear combinations. Matrices represent those maps after bases are chosen. Shapes, subspaces, inner products and factorizations answer different questions: a linear map need not preserve distance, angle, rank or even information about its input.
outcomes: Distinguish linearity, invertibility, area preservation and orthogonality.
Navigate from vector-space structure to geometry and numerical computation.

sources.label: MIT 18.06: linear transformations and their matrices

labs.summary: A shear keeps the area while tipping the ruler.
labs.assumptions: Real two-dimensional column vectors in the standard orthonormal basis; Euclidean lengths and angles. The unit square is mapped vertex by vertex by S. Both graph axes use the same scale. The shear coefficient varies while the second coordinate is unchanged. This family is invertible with determinant one for every real s; it illustrates a particular linear map, not a property of all matrices.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Linear algebra. Real two-dimensional column vectors in the standard orthonormal basis; Euclidean lengths and angles. The unit square is mapped vertex by vertex by S. Both graph axes use the same scale. The shear coefficient varies while the second coordinate is unchanged. This family is invertible with determinant one for every real s; it illustrates a particular linear map, not a property of all matrices. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Ask what the map preserves. Linearity, invertibility, volume preservation and orthogonality are different properties, with different mathematical checks.

title: Linear independence
summary: Vectors are linearly independent when their zero linear combination requires every coefficient to be zero. Equivalently, no vector in the set is a linear combination of the others.
outcomes: Exhibit a nontrivial zero combination to prove dependence.
Separate exact independence from numerical resolvability.

labs.title: Collapse a dimension
labs.summary: If a direction adds no new reach, its coefficient is redundant.
labs.assumptions: Two real columns u=(1,1) and v=(1,1+ε). Independence is evaluated in exact arithmetic; near-zero ε can be numerically difficult even when nonzero.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Linear independence. Two real columns u=(1,1) and v=(1,1+ε). Independence is evaluated in exact arithmetic; near-zero ε can be numerically difficult even when nonzero. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: At ε=0 the parallelogram collapses to a line. At small nonzero ε the columns are independent but nearly redundant numerically.

title: Local minima, global minima, and saddle points
summary: A local minimizer has no worse objective value than nearby feasible points; a global minimizer has no worse value than any feasible point. A saddle has both higher and lower values arbitrarily nearby. For a smooth unconstrained problem, zero gradient identifies a stationary candidate—not which of these roles it plays.
outcomes: Classify stationary points using local curvature.
Explain why a global-optimality conclusion needs more than a small gradient or a local plot.

title: Log-normal
summary: A positive random variable is log-normal when its natural logarithm is Gaussian. Parameters μ and σ describe the logarithm, not the mean and standard deviation of the original variable.
outcomes: Interpret log-normal parameters on the right scale.
Distinguish mean, median, and mode after exponentiation.

labs.summary: Multiplication in ordinary space becomes addition in log space.

labs.accessibilitySummary: Log-normal. μ=0 while σ changes. X is a dimensionless multiplicative factor. The displayed density ends at 12, but the right tail continues indefinitely. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Exponentiating the log mean gives the median, not the arithmetic mean; the latter grows with log-space variance.

title: Low-rank approximation
summary: Truncating an SVD to its k largest singular values gives a best rank-at-most-k approximation in spectral and Frobenius norms. The discarded singular values quantify the approximation error.

title: Markov chains
summary: A discrete-time Markov chain describes a state sequence whose next-state distribution, conditional on the current state, does not depend on earlier states.
outcomes: Propagate a distribution through a transition matrix.
Separate stationarity, uniqueness, and convergence instead of assuming they are equivalent.

labs.title: Markov chains: calculate and compare
labs.summary: Move probability mass along outgoing transitions, then add the arrivals.
labs.assumptions: Two states A and B; row distributions; a fixed transition matrix with nonnegative rows summing to 1. The initial distribution is π₀=(1,0).
labs.accessibilitySummary: Markov chains. Two states A and B; row distributions; a fixed transition matrix with nonnegative rows summing to 1. The initial distribution is π₀=(1,0). A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: The row vector after t transitions is π₀Pᵗ. For this irreducible, aperiodic chain it approaches (2/3,1/3).

title: Markov processes
summary: A Markov process makes its future conditionally independent of its past given the present state. Time and state can be discrete or continuous. This lesson studies a two-state continuous-time chain, where transition rates and exponential holding times replace the fixed-step transition probabilities used in the discrete-time Markov-chain lesson.
outcomes: Translate continuous-time rates into probability dynamics.
Distinguish jump frequencies, holding times and stationary occupancy.

sources.label: Art Owen: stochastic processes and simulation

labs.title: Rates move probability through continuous time
labs.summary: The state forgets how it arrived, but the clock still matters.
labs.equation: Q=[[-α,α],[β,−β]], α=0.5/h; p′=pQ; P(failed at t|working at 0)=α(1−e⁻⁽α⁺β⁾ᵗ)/(α+β)
labs.assumptions: A time-homogeneous continuous-time chain with states working and failed, failure rate α=0.5 per hour and repair rate β>0 per hour. It starts working with probability one. Curves show exact state probabilities, not a single machine's jump path. Row-vector probabilities multiply the generator Q on the right.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Markov processes. A time-homogeneous continuous-time chain with states working and failed, failure rate α=0.5 per hour and repair rate β>0 per hour. It starts working with probability one. Curves show exact state probabilities, not a single machine's jump path. Row-vector probabilities multiply the generator Q on the right. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: A generator contains rates with units and rows summing to zero. A finite-time transition matrix contains probabilities and rows summing to one.

title: Mathematical foundations
summary: Mathematics makes a learning system's assumptions inspectable. Linear algebra defines representations, calculus describes sensitivity, probability models uncertainty, statistics connects observations to claims, optimization searches for decisions, information theory studies representation limits, and discrete mathematics supports proofs and computational analysis. Use the branch that answers your current question, then connect it to its prerequisites.
outcomes: Connect representation, loss, derivatives and optimization in one inspectable example.
Choose an appropriate mathematical route while keeping empirical claims separate.

sources.label: Mathematics for Machine Learning: subject map and open textbook
Stanford EE364A: gradient methods and step selection

Start from w₀=0 and take exactly one full-gradient update. The slider changes the step size; data and objective stay fixed. No stochastic sampling, regularization or held-out evaluation is included. Arithmetic is a small deterministic calculation, not model training on a real dataset.

title: Mathematical induction
summary: Mathematical induction proves a statement across a well-founded sequence by establishing a base case and a step that carries truth to the next case. It is a deductive argument, not extrapolation from many successful examples. The statement being carried forward must be precise enough to support that step.
outcomes: Separate a base case, induction hypothesis and arbitrary inductive step.
Translate a concrete growth picture into a general algebraic proof.

sources.label: MIT Mathematics for Computer Science: induction
MIT Mathematics for Computer Science: patterns of proof

labs.summary: The border changes with n; the reason it completes a square does not.

Solid cells form the previous (n−1)×(n−1) square; the striped right column and bottom row add 2n−1 cells, counting their shared corner once. The slider only renders n=1,…,10; the general proof is symbolic and does not depend on exhausting that finite display range. No empirical inference or probabilistic claim is made.

title: Matrix calculus
summary: Matrix calculus organizes derivatives with respect to array-valued parameters. For a scalar loss, the gradient has the parameter's shape and converts a small parameter perturbation into a first-order change in loss.
outcomes: Derive the squared-error matrix gradient.
Separate a one-parameter slice from the full gradient.

title: Matrix multiplication and tensor contraction
summary: Matrix multiplication sums products over a shared inner axis. Tensor contraction extends this idea to specified axes of higher-order arrays while preserving the remaining axes.
outcomes: Derive output shape and one matrix-product entry.
Distinguish contraction, broadcasting, and elementwise multiplication.

labs.takeaway: The contracted index disappears from the output. Changing multiplication order generally changes both the transformation and the result.

title: Maximum a posteriori estimation
summary: MAP selects a mode of a posterior density in a specified parameterization. It combines log likelihood and log prior, but summarizes the posterior with only one location. Continuous density modes can change under reparameterization and need not equal posterior means.
outcomes: Calculate a beta-posterior mode and distinguish it from its mean.
Explain why MAP depends on parameter coordinates.

labs.summary: The highest point depends on the ruler used for density.

labs.takeaway: Report the parameterization and distinguish MAP, posterior mean and posterior uncertainty; they answer different questions.

title: Maximum likelihood estimation
summary: Maximum likelihood chooses a parameter maximizing the likelihood of the observed data under a specified model. For continuous data the likelihood is a density evaluated at those data, not the probability of observing that exact point. It is not generally a probability distribution over parameters.
outcomes: Derive the Bernoulli maximum-likelihood estimate, including endpoints.
Distinguish likelihood, probability density and posterior probability.

labs.takeaway: A likelihood peak identifies a best fit within the model; its height is not posterior probability or a goodness-of-fit certificate.

title: Mini-batch optimization
summary: A minibatch gradient averages several per-example gradients evaluated at the same parameter state. It changes estimator variance, hardware utilization and the number of updates per data pass. Its statistical behavior depends on how examples are sampled, not just on the numerical batch size.
outcomes: Compute an exact minibatch-gradient distribution.
Distinguish independent-sampling variance from finite-population variance.

labs.takeaway: Averaging reduces sampling variability, but the finite-population correction matters: drawing all four distinct examples has zero variance, unlike four independent draws with replacement.

title: Minimum description length
summary: Minimum description length selects explanations by how concisely they encode data under a declared coding scheme. In a two-part code, the description includes both the model and the data conditional on it. Improving fit is useful only if the data savings compensate for the extra model description.
outcomes: Compare complete two-part descriptions rather than likelihood alone.
Distinguish sequence coding, count coding and parameter overhead.

Lines join integer-count results only as a visual guide.

title: Missing-data mechanisms
summary: A missing-data mechanism describes how observation indicators depend on observed and unobserved values. MCAR removes dependence on data values; MAR allows dependence on observed information but not on the missing values after conditioning on that information. MNAR retains dependence on unobserved values. These are assumptions about the observation process, not labels determined by the percentage missing.
outcomes: State MCAR, MAR and MNAR relative to explicitly observed variables.
Explain why equal missingness rates can give different biases and why adjustment can fail within observed groups.

title: Momentum and adaptive methods
summary: Momentum carries information from earlier gradients into the next update. Adaptive methods instead also change coordinate-wise step scales using gradient statistics. These mechanisms can be combined, but they are not interchangeable and neither guarantees faster convergence on every objective.
outcomes: Compute a heavy-ball update and explain an overshoot.
Separate temporal momentum from coordinate-wise adaptive scaling.

labs.summary: A small current gradient does not erase the velocity already accumulated.

labs.takeaway: Momentum changes the dynamics, not just the current step length. Crossing the optimum can be compatible with convergence, and larger β can also leave more residual oscillation.

title: Monte Carlo estimation
summary: Monte Carlo estimation approximates an expectation by an average of random evaluations. Under IID sampling and finite variance, the sample mean is unbiased and its variance falls in proportion to 1/n. This describes repeated-sampling behavior, not a guarantee that one running estimate moves monotonically toward the answer.
outcomes: Derive Monte Carlo variance for a known integrand.
Separate realized error, estimated standard error and exact reference uncertainty.

labs.takeaway: More IID samples reduce estimator variance. They do not guarantee a smaller realized error at every increment.

title: Multinomial
summary: The multinomial distribution models category counts from n independent categorical trials with a shared probability vector. The counts sum to n and are dependent even though the trials are independent.
outcomes: Compute a multinomial joint probability.

title: Multiple testing
summary: Testing many hypotheses creates more opportunities for false discoveries. Family-wise error is the probability of at least one false rejection in a defined family. Bonferroni controls it by testing each of m hypotheses at α/m when the individual null p-values are valid, without requiring independence.
outcomes: Compute the accumulation of false-rejection risk under independence.
Derive Bonferroni's guarantee and distinguish FWER from FDR.

title: Multivariate Gaussian
summary: A multivariate Gaussian models a vector using a mean and covariance matrix. For positive-definite covariance, equal-density contours are ellipsoids determined by Mahalanobis distance, not by independent coordinatewise error bars.
outcomes: Interpret Gaussian covariance contours.
Separate marginal spread from joint probability coverage.

title: Mutual information
summary: Mutual information measures how far a joint distribution is from the product of its marginals. For discrete variables it equals the average reduction in uncertainty from observing the other variable. It is symmetric and detects dependence that a linear correlation coefficient can miss; it does not establish causation.
outcomes: Calculate MI for a nonlinear relationship with zero correlation.
Separate statistical dependence, information units and causal interpretation.

title: Newton and quasi-Newton methods
summary: Newton's method uses a local Hessian to turn a gradient into a curvature-aware direction. Quasi-Newton methods such as BFGS learn a curvature approximation from successive parameter and gradient differences. Their extra information can reduce iterations, but each iteration has costs and may require safeguards.
outcomes: Derive a Newton direction from a local quadratic model.
Distinguish exact Newton curvature, BFGS updates and limited-memory storage.

labs.takeaway: Newton solves a local quadratic model. A trustworthy implementation solves for the direction and controls the step; it does not assume every Hessian is invertible or every full step is safe.

title: Numerical conditioning
summary: Conditioning measures a problem's sensitivity to input perturbations. For an invertible matrix, κ₂(A)=σmax/σmin bounds worst-case relative amplification in a linear solve when only the right-hand side changes.
outcomes: Compute and interpret a condition number.
Distinguish input sensitivity, residuals, and algorithmic stability.

labs.assumptions: A=diag(1,ε), b=(1,0), δb=(0,0.001), with A held fixed and Euclidean relative errors. Here 0<ε≤1, so κ₂=1/ε. The example attains the bound.

labs.takeaway: Conditioning belongs to the problem; numerical stability belongs to the algorithm. A stable algorithm cannot remove sensitivity already present in the data.

title: Numerical stability
summary: Numerical stability concerns how an algorithm handles rounding and other small computational errors. Conditioning concerns how the mathematical answer changes when its input changes. Equivalent exact formulas can behave very differently in finite precision, even for a well-conditioned problem.

Separate mathematical conditioning, algorithm stability and displayed precision.

title: Objectives, losses, and cost functions
summary: A loss scores a prediction against an outcome. A training objective aggregates those losses and may add penalties or constraints. Terminology varies, so an implementation should state the complete expression, its reduction, and the variables being optimized rather than rely on the word cost.
outcomes: Distinguish an individual loss from the full training objective.
Explain why squared, absolute and Huber losses choose different constant predictions.

sources.label: Dive into Deep Learning: linear regression
scikit-learn: linear models, penalties and robust regression

labs.title: Change the loss, change the answer
labs.summary: The optimizer answers the question encoded by the loss—not the question you meant to ask.
labs.equation: J(c)=¼Σᵢℓ(c−yᵢ); ℓ₂(r)=r²/2; ℓ₁(r)=|r|; Huber₁(r)=r²/2 if |r|≤1, else |r|−½
labs.assumptions: Four equally weighted, dimensionless observations y={−1,0,1,5}; every observation receives the same constant prediction. The three curves use different losses, all averaged over four examples. Their heights are not interchangeable quality scores. This lab fixes Huber's threshold at 1 and does not estimate a scale parameter.

The three curves use different losses, all averaged over four examples. Their heights are not interchangeable quality scores. labs.takeaway: Loss choice changes which prediction is optimal. Averaging, weighting, clipping and regularization are part of the mathematical specification, not implementation trivia.

title: Online algorithms
summary: An online algorithm commits to actions as requests arrive, without knowing future requests. Competitive analysis compares its total cost with an offline optimum that knows the entire sequence. The comparison is over all allowed sequences, not merely the typical future in a training dataset.
outcomes: Analyze a threshold policy against a clairvoyant offline optimum.
Distinguish competitive analysis, regret and forecast-based expected performance.

sources.label: CMU 15-850: online algorithms and ski rental

labs.title: Buy before you know when the season ends
labs.summary: The worst time for the season to end is often the day you finally buy.
labs.equation: ALG_d(T)=T if T<d, else d−1+8; OPT(T)=min(T,8)
labs.assumptions: Time is discrete, T is a positive integer, rental costs one credit per day and purchase costs eight credits. On the purchase day you buy instead of renting. A deterministic threshold policy rents on days 1 through d−1 and buys if day d arrives. No resale, interest, discounts or forecasts are included. The chart shows T=1…24, while the worst-case ratio is derived over all positive integer horizons. Future T is not an input available to the policy.

The chart shows T=1…24, while the worst-case ratio is derived over all positive integer horizons. Future T is not an input available to the policy. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Choose a rule before seeing the future, name the offline benchmark, and evaluate the worst allowed stopping point. For this discrete model, buying on day eight guarantees 15/8, not exactly two.

title: Optimization
summary: Optimization selects decision variables to minimize or maximize a specified objective over a feasible set. The model defines what counts as a good answer; the algorithm attempts to find it. Smoothness, convexity, constraints and numerical conditioning determine which guarantees and computational methods apply.
outcomes: Separate optimization variables and hyperparameters from solver controls.
Certify a nonsmooth convex optimum and interpret its fit–penalty tradeoff.

sources.label: Parikh and Boyd: proximal algorithms and soft thresholding
Stanford STATS 305B: LASSO, subgradients and proximal updates

labs.title: The best fit is not always the best objective
labs.summary: Changing the penalty moves the target; changing a step size changes how you approach it.
labs.assumptions: One real decision variable w, fixed target value 3, squared-error fit with coefficient one half, and a nonnegative absolute-value penalty weight λ. There are no explicit constraints. The exact minimizer is calculated analytically, not obtained by an iterative optimizer. At λ>0 the objective has a kink at zero. This scalar model illustrates objective structure; it does not measure predictive generalization or choose λ from data.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Optimization. One real decision variable w, fixed target value 3, squared-error fit with coefficient one half, and a nonnegative absolute-value penalty weight λ. There are no explicit constraints. The exact minimizer is calculated analytically, not obtained by an iterative optimizer. At λ>0 the objective has a kink at zero. This scalar model illustrates objective structure; it does not measure predictive generalization or choose λ from data. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Separate problem specification, optimality conditions and algorithm behavior. A penalty can make zero optimal at a nondifferentiable point; ordinary zero-gradient reasoning is then insufficient.

title: Ordinary differential equations
summary: An ordinary differential equation specifies how a state changes with one independent variable, often time. An initial condition selects a trajectory when appropriate existence and uniqueness conditions hold. A numerical solver approximates that trajectory; its discrete dynamics can behave differently from the continuous equation.
outcomes: Separate the continuous initial-value problem from a numerical update rule.
Explain why stability, positivity and accuracy impose different conditions.

sources.label: OpenStax: initial-value problems and differential equations

labs.summary: The model can decay while the numerical method explodes.

labs.assumptions: Time is measured in seconds and the decay rate is 2 per second. State is normalized. The vertical axis adapts to include unstable numerical values.

labs.takeaway: Choose a numerical step with accuracy, stability and physical constraints in mind. A correct differential equation does not make every discretization reliable.

title: Orthogonality and orthonormal bases
summary: Orthogonal vectors have zero inner product. An orthonormal basis combines orthogonality with unit lengths, making coordinates obtainable by inner products and preserving Euclidean lengths under a square basis change.
outcomes: Read coordinates in an orthonormal basis using inner products.
Distinguish an orthogonal change of basis from a subspace projection.

labs.summary: Independent unit rulers let you read each coordinate directly.
labs.equation: QᵀQ=I; c=Qᵀx; ‖c‖₂=‖x‖₂ for square orthogonal Q
labs.assumptions: Q is a real 2×2 rotation matrix with columns (cosθ,sinθ) and (−sinθ,cosθ). The fixed vector is x=(2,1). Both coordinate axes use the same scale.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Orthogonality and orthonormal bases. Q is a real 2×2 rotation matrix with columns (cosθ,sinθ) and (−sinθ,cosθ). The fixed vector is x=(2,1). Both coordinate axes use the same scale. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: The basis rotates and the coordinate values change, while x's squared length stays five. Orthogonal columns alone need normalization before Qᵀ gives inverse coordinates.

title: p-values and statistical power
summary: A p-value evaluates how extreme an observed statistic is under a null model using a specified tail rule. Power instead describes how often a fixed test rejects under a specified alternative before observing a new sample. Neither quantity is the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
outcomes: Calculate a one-sided p-value and a distinct power curve.
Reject posterior and effect-size interpretations of a p-value.

sources.label: NIST: planning sample size from size and power

labs.title: One observed p-value, many powers
labs.summary: The p-value looks back at data; power looks across possible datasets.
labs.assumptions: The observed count is fixed at 15 successes in 20 independent trials. The prechosen upper-tail rejection rule is K≥15. The slider changes the alternative used to calculate power, not the observed dataset or its null p-value.
labs.accessibilitySummary: p-values and statistical power. The observed count is fixed at 15 successes in 20 independent trials. The prechosen upper-tail rejection rule is K≥15. The slider changes the alternative used to calculate power, not the observed dataset or its null p-value. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Keep observed evidence, planned error control, practical effect size and power at plausible alternatives as separate reported quantities.

title: P, NP, NP-hard, and NP-complete
summary: P and NP classify decision problems by polynomial-time solving and verification. NP-hardness describes reduction-based difficulty, while NP-completeness combines hardness with membership in NP. These are properties of problem families and encodings, not labels inferred from one slow instance or a small interactive example.
outcomes: Distinguish P, NP, NP-hard and NP-complete without assuming P≠NP.
Separate witness verification, instance solving and a hardness proof.

Clay Mathematics Institute: P versus NP
Stephen Cook: official P versus NP problem description

labs.summary: A failed assignment rejects that witness, not the existence of every witness.

The lab always evaluates every literal, without short-circuiting, and displays all eight assignments. Stripes mark satisfying assignments; a thick border marks the selected certificate. This formula is 2-CNF, a tractable SAT subclass. The finite gallery illustrates certificate verification, not a proof that the illustrated subclass is NP-complete or that exhaustive search is necessary.

A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Efficiently checking a proposed yes-certificate does not supply one. NP-complete means both in NP and NP-hard; it does not mean proven exponential time.

title: Parameters and decision variables
summary: Decision variables are the quantities an optimization problem is allowed to choose. In model fitting these often include weights and intercepts, while inputs and observed labels are held fixed. A model parameter can also be frozen; being stored in a model does not automatically make it trainable.
outcomes: Identify which quantities a stated fitting problem may change.
Separate trainability, parameter identifiability and numerical optimization.

sources.label: Dive into Deep Learning: linear regression
Boyd and Vandenberghe: optimization variables and problem formulations

labs.title: Move the model, keep the data fixed
labs.summary: Before asking for the best answer, say which knobs the solver may turn.

labs.accessibilitySummary: Parameters and decision variables. Three fixed observations (−1,−1), (0,1), and (1,3). Only w is optimized; b is deliberately frozen at 1. Dots show observations, the adjustable line shows predictions, and the comparison line uses the exact optimum w=2. Feature and target values are dimensionless. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: The set of trainable variables defines the feasible family of models. A loss gradient for one parameter says nothing about a frozen quantity unless it is explicitly included in the optimization problem.

title: Perplexity
summary: Perplexity exponentiates average negative log likelihood. For a specified tokenization and evaluation protocol, lower values mean higher probability assigned to the observed sequence.
outcomes: Convert mean log loss into perplexity using the correct base.
Identify when two perplexity scores do not share an evaluation protocol.

sources.label: MacKay: Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms
Jurafsky and Martin: Speech and Language Processing

labs.title: Perplexity: calculate and compare
labs.summary: Average surprise becomes an equivalent branching factor when you exponentiate it.
labs.equation: PPL=exp(−(1/N)Σₜ ln q(xₜ|x<ₜ)) = 2ᴴ when H is in bits
labs.assumptions: Toy two-token source: independent tokens with P(token 1)=0.7. The curve is population perplexity 2 raised to binary cross-entropy, not a measured language-model benchmark.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Perplexity. Toy two-token source: independent tokens with P(token 1)=0.7. The curve is population perplexity 2 raised to binary cross-entropy, not a measured language-model benchmark. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: A uniform two-token model has perplexity 2; a well-matched nonuniform model can have perplexity below 2.

title: Point estimation
summary: A point estimator is a rule that maps a sample to a parameter value. Its realized output is an estimate. Calling an estimator best requires a model, a loss function and a comparison criterion; a single number does not convey its uncertainty.
outcomes: Distinguish a random estimator from its realized estimate.
Evaluate a sample proportion using a specified squared-error criterion.

sources.label: Taboga: point estimation, loss and risk

labs.title: One estimate, many possible samples
labs.summary: The observed dot is fixed; the procedure has a distribution.
labs.assumptions: Ten independent Bernoulli(p) observations with common, fixed p. Bars enumerate the sampling distribution of K/10. The marked p is known only inside this explanatory model; a real analyst does not get to set the population truth.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Point estimation. Ten independent Bernoulli(p) observations with common, fixed p. Bars enumerate the sampling distribution of K/10. The marked p is known only inside this explanatory model; a real analyst does not get to set the population truth. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Evaluate the rule across possible samples, not by whether one realized estimate looks plausible.

title: Poisson
summary: A Poisson distribution assigns probabilities to nonnegative integer counts with mean and variance λ. Counts from a homogeneous Poisson process over duration t have λ=rate×t; rarity alone does not establish this model.
outcomes: Convert rate and exposure into a Poisson parameter.
Check the model's mean–variance and process assumptions.

labs.title: Count arrivals in a fixed window
labs.summary: Fix the observation window; let the count vary.
labs.assumptions: λ is the expected count in one fixed interval, not a probability. The graph shows k=0…30 and reports omitted upper-tail mass without rescaling the bars. At λ=0, all mass is at zero.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Poisson. λ is the expected count in one fixed interval, not a probability. The graph shows k=0…30 and reports omitted upper-tail mass without rescaling the bars. At λ=0, all mass is at zero. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: A count's mean and variance being equal is a Poisson property, not a rule for all event-count data.

title: Populations and samples
summary: A population is the set of units or generating distribution about which a claim is intended. A sample is the subset actually observed. A statistic summarizes the sample; a parameter describes the target. Inference requires a link between them, supplied by a sampling design or explicit modeling assumptions—not just by having many rows.
outcomes: Distinguish population, sampling frame, sample, parameter and statistic.
Read an exact sampling distribution and separate sampling variation from coverage bias.

sources.label: Penn State STAT 506: population mean and sampling designs
Penn State STAT 506: nonsampling error and nonresponse

labs.title: Six possible samples, one target population
labs.summary: More samples from the wrong frame still describe the wrong frame.

labs.assumptions: The finite target population has four distinct units with values (2,4,8,10) score units. Simple random sampling without replacement selects two units: all six unordered pairs are equally likely. The control selects a pair for inspection, not a random draw or an ordered collection process. A comparison design samples two units uniformly from an incomplete frame containing only (2,4,8). Both plotted distributions are exhaustive calculations. S² uses denominator N−1 for the finite population.

The control selects a pair for inspection, not a random draw or an ordered collection process. A comparison design samples two units uniformly from an incomplete frame containing only (2,4,8). Both plotted distributions are exhaustive calculations. S² uses denominator N−1 for the finite population. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Sampling variation and coverage error are different. An unbiased procedure can miss in one sample; a systematically incomplete frame can miss even when measured perfectly.

title: Positive-semidefinite matrices
summary: A real symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite when its quadratic form is nonnegative in every direction. Equivalently, all its eigenvalues are nonnegative. Covariance and Gram matrices have this structure.
outcomes: Relate quadratic forms, eigenvalues, and Gram matrices.
Distinguish PSD, positive definite, and indefinite matrices.

labs.title: Sweep the quadratic form
labs.summary: Sweep every direction: a PSD matrix never dips below zero.
labs.equation: A⪰0 ⇔ xᵀAx≥0 for all x ⇔ λmin(A)≥0, for symmetric A
labs.assumptions: A=diag(1,t). The graph evaluates the quadratic form on unit vectors (cosθ,sinθ); opposite directions give the same value.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Positive-semidefinite matrices. A=diag(1,t). The graph evaluates the quadratic form on unit vectors (cosθ,sinθ); opposite directions give the same value. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Positive entries are neither necessary nor sufficient for positive semidefiniteness. The condition concerns all directions, not individual cells.

title: Posterior predictive distributions
summary: A posterior predictive distribution averages the sampling distribution of future observations over the posterior of model parameters. It includes future observation noise and remaining parameter uncertainty, conditional on the assumed model and observed data.
outcomes: Calculate an exact beta-binomial posterior predictive.
Explain why shared parameter uncertainty changes joint future outcomes.

labs.title: Predict with a distribution of probabilities
labs.summary: Draw one uncertain probability, then a future batch.
labs.assumptions: The current posterior is p|data~Beta(3,2), so μ=0.6. Future trials are conditionally independent given that same p. Grouped bars compare the exact beta-binomial predictive with Binomial(m,0.6); both display the complete count support. The shared vertical scale follows the larger peak as m changes.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Posterior predictive distributions. The current posterior is p|data~Beta(3,2), so μ=0.6. Future trials are conditionally independent given that same p. Grouped bars compare the exact beta-binomial predictive with Binomial(m,0.6); both display the complete count support. The shared vertical scale follows the larger peak as m changes. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Plugging in a posterior mean may get the expected count right while understating uncertainty about a whole future batch.

title: Probability
summary: Probability starts with a sample space, events and a consistent assignment of mass. Random variables map outcomes to quantities. A joint model specifies how several quantities vary together; marginals describe them separately. Conditioning, expectations and distributions are operations on that model—not permission to assume independence.
outcomes: Derive a sum distribution from a joint probability table.
Identify which expectation and variance identities require independence.

labs.title: Two fair marginals, three different worlds
labs.summary: Knowing each coin is fair does not tell you how often they agree.
labs.assumptions: X and Y each take values zero or one. Rows of the joint table index X and columns index Y. q lies in [0,1/2], making all four masses nonnegative and summing to one. Every marginal is Bernoulli(1/2), but the pair is independent only at q=1/4. S=X+Y. These are exact probabilities, not finite sample frequencies; no physical coin-toss independence is assumed.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Probability. X and Y each take values zero or one. Every marginal is Bernoulli(1/2), but the pair is independent only at q=1/4. S=X+Y. These are exact probabilities, not finite sample frequencies; no physical coin-toss independence is assumed. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Marginals do not determine a joint distribution. Before multiplying probabilities or using an independent-sum formula, inspect the dependence assumptions.

title: Probability mass and density functions
summary: A PMF assigns probability to individual discrete outcomes. A PDF assigns density to a continuous variable: interval probability is an integral, while any individual point has probability zero for an absolutely continuous distribution.
outcomes: Distinguish PMF sums from PDF areas.
Explain why density can exceed one without violating probability axioms.

labs.title: Height is not probability
labs.summary: For a density, measure the area—not the height.
labs.equation: P(X=k)=p(k); P(a≤X≤b)=∫ₐᵇf(x)dx for an absolutely continuous X
labs.assumptions: The graph is Uniform(0,b), not a PMF. The shaded interval is the left half of its support. Density has inverse-length units; probability is dimensionless.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Probability mass and density functions. The graph is Uniform(0,b), not a PMF. The shaded interval is the left half of its support. Density has inverse-length units; probability is dimensionless. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: A density may exceed one. Its integral, not its height, must equal one; mixed distributions need both atomic masses and a continuous part.

title: Product, quotient, and chain rules
summary: Differentiation rules combine local derivatives while preserving how expressions depend on an input. Products have two first-order contributions, quotients must account for denominator change, and compositions multiply sensitivities along their dependency path.
outcomes: Derive a quotient derivative by combining product and chain rules.
Account for every path by which an input affects the output.

labs.title: Two moving parts in a quotient
labs.summary: Every path by which x changes the output must contribute to the derivative.
labs.assumptions: The plotted quotient is r(x)=(x²+1)/(x+2). Its numerator and denominator are differentiable and the denominator is nonzero throughout the displayed interval [−1,2]. Curves show the two derivative contributions and their sum, not the quotient's value. The singular point x=−2 is outside the lab domain.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Product, quotient, and chain rules. The plotted quotient is r(x)=(x²+1)/(x+2). Its numerator and denominator are differentiable and the denominator is nonzero throughout the displayed interval [−1,2]. Curves show the two derivative contributions and their sum, not the quotient's value. The singular point x=−2 is outside the lab domain. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Differentiate the dependency structure, not the expression's appearance. A missing denominator or inner-function contribution can give a plausible-looking but incorrect slope.

title: Projections
summary: An orthogonal projection maps a vector to the closest point in a linear subspace under Euclidean distance. Its residual lies perpendicular to every direction in that subspace.
outcomes: Compute a projection and its orthogonal residual.
Connect projection geometry with least-squares fitting and numerical stability.

labs.title: Projection and residual
labs.summary: Keep the component along the subspace; leave a perpendicular residual.
labs.assumptions: Project x=(2,1) onto the line spanned by the real unit vector u=(cosθ,sinθ). The displayed residual joins the projected endpoint to x.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Projections. Project x=(2,1) onto the line spanned by the real unit vector u=(cosθ,sinθ). The displayed residual joins the projected endpoint to x. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Projection length and residual length trade off, but their squared lengths add to ‖x‖²=5 because the components are orthogonal.

title: Proof by contradiction
summary: In classical logic, proof by contradiction establishes a proposition by assuming its negation and deriving an impossibility from that assumption plus the premises. The contradiction must be a logical conflict, not merely an unexpected result. Tracking exactly which assumption is rejected is part of the proof.
outcomes: Identify the negated assumption and the precise contradiction.
Separate a universal counting guarantee from one example or a probabilistic claim.

MIT Mathematics for Computer Science: cardinality and pigeonhole rules

labs.title: The fifth item breaks the no-collision assumption
labs.summary: If four buckets each held at most one item, where could a fifth item go?
labs.equation: no collision ⇒ Σⱼ₌₁⁴ loadⱼ≤4; n>4 contradicts this; maxⱼ loadⱼ≥⌈n/4⌉
labs.assumptions: Every one of n distinct items is assigned to exactly one of four buckets. Buckets have no physical capacity limit. The displayed assignment is deterministic round-robin, not random sampling: item i goes to bucket 1+((i−1) mod 4). Numbered cells identify items; stripes mark additional items in an already used bucket. Twelve display slots cover the slider's maximum and are not a constraint in the theorem. The universal bound follows from counting, not from this one assignment.

The displayed assignment is deterministic round-robin, not random sampling: item i goes to bucket 1+((i−1) mod 4). Numbered cells identify items; stripes mark additional items in an already used bucket. Twelve display slots cover the slider's maximum and are not a constraint in the theorem. The universal bound follows from counting, not from this one assignment. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: An impossible capacity bound rejects the no-collision assumption for every assignment. A single crowded picture illustrates the result but does not prove its universality.

title: Random variables
summary: A real random variable is a measurable function from outcomes to real numbers. Its distribution is the probability assigned to sets of resulting values. The function is fixed; the outcome supplied to it is uncertain. General random elements may instead take values such as categories or functions.
outcomes: Construct a distribution from an outcome mapping.
Distinguish a random variable, its distribution and an observation.

labs.summary: Map outcomes first, then collect their probability mass.

labs.accessibilitySummary: Random variables. Two independent flips have the same head probability p. X counts heads: TT→0, TH→1, HT→1, HH→2. The table lists elementary outcomes; bars aggregate their probabilities by X. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: The distribution of a random variable is not the sample space: different outcomes can map to the same value.

title: Randomized algorithms
summary: A randomized algorithm uses internal random choices, so its output or resource use can vary even for a fixed input. Monte Carlo algorithms allow a controlled error probability; Las Vegas algorithms return correct answers but have random resource use. The distribution of those internal choices belongs in the algorithm's specification.
outcomes: Distinguish internal randomization from random-input analysis.
Explain when independent repetition reduces one-sided error and when it does not.

labs.summary: Checking the same blind spot twelve times still leaves the same blind spot.
labs.equation: Check A(Br)=Cr; P(all k pass | fixed AB≠C) ≤ 2⁻ᵏ
labs.assumptions: A=[[1,2],[3,4]], B=[[2,0],[1,2]] and the incorrect claimed product is C=[[5,3],[10,8]]. Each fresh r is uniform on {(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)} and independent across checks. Exact integer arithmetic is used. Two vectors miss this particular error, making the bound an equality here. The comparison policy draws one vector and reuses it. The plotted values are exact probabilities, not sampled runs; k=0 means accept with no checks.

Each fresh r is uniform on {(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)} and independent across checks. Exact integer arithmetic is used. Two vectors miss this particular error, making the bound an equality here. The comparison policy draws one vector and reuses it. The plotted values are exact probabilities, not sampled runs; k=0 means accept with no checks. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Error amplification needs the stated independence and error model. Repeated computation is not necessarily repeated evidence, and a false-pass bound is not a posterior correctness probability.

title: Rank and null space
summary: The rank of A:Rⁿ→Rᵐ is the dimension of its image. Its null space contains inputs mapped to zero. Rank plus nullity equals n, the dimension of the domain.
outcomes: Use rank-nullity with the correct domain dimension.
Describe nonunique solutions using a null-space basis.

labs.title: Which directions disappear?
labs.summary: Count the directions that survive and the directions that disappear.
labs.assumptions: A maps R³ into R². The third input coordinate always disappears. At t=0 the second coordinate disappears as well. Rank is evaluated in exact arithmetic.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Rank and null space. A maps R³ into R². The third input coordinate always disappears. At t=0 the second coordinate disappears as well. Rank is evaluated in exact arithmetic. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: A nontrivial null space means different inputs can produce the same output. In this example the domain dimension is three, not the number of matrix rows.

title: Rate-distortion theory
summary: Rate-distortion theory asks for the minimum asymptotic communication rate needed to reconstruct a source within a specified distortion budget. Its answer depends on the source distribution, the distortion function and the coding setting—not just on a desired file size or an informal notion of perceptual quality.
outcomes: Calculate the fair-binary Hamming rate-distortion curve.
Explain the zero-rate plateau and the role of coding assumptions.

labs.title: How many bits buy a distortion budget?
labs.summary: Once a constant answer meets the error budget, sending more is optional.
labs.equation: R(D)=minₚ(x̂|x): E[d(X,X̂)]≤D I(X;X̂); fair binary/Hamming: R(D)=1−h₂(D) for D≤½, else 0
labs.assumptions: IID fair binary source, binary reconstructions, Hamming distortion 1 when a reconstructed bit is wrong and 0 otherwise. Rate is bits per source symbol under asymptotically long block coding. The slider is an upper bound on average error, not an instruction to introduce exactly that much error.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Rate-distortion theory. IID fair binary source, binary reconstructions, Hamming distortion 1 when a reconstructed bit is wrong and 0 otherwise. Rate is bits per source symbol under asymptotically long block coding. The slider is an upper bound on average error, not an instruction to introduce exactly that much error. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: A distortion budget enlarges the feasible coding set, so the minimum rate cannot increase as the budget grows.

title: Recurrence relations
summary: A recurrence specifies a quantity through smaller instances and boundary values. It can define a sequence or model an algorithm's work; those are different quantities. The model must say what n measures, which calls occur, and what work remains outside those calls.
outcomes: Translate a recursive decomposition into a well-specified work recurrence.
Reconcile recursion-level totals, base cases and a proved closed form.

sources.label: Cornell CS 3110: analyzing running time with recurrences
MIT Mathematics for Computer Science: induction

labs.title: Smaller calls, the same bill at every level
labs.summary: Halving each job does not halve the level's work when the number of jobs doubles.
labs.assumptions: This is an exact toy work model on positive powers of two, not a benchmark or an exact merge-sort comparison count. Each non-leaf call makes two half-size calls and incurs its own size in additional work units. A size-one call costs one unit. Depth zero is the root; depth k contains the leaves. Bars aggregate work at a depth, not the number of calls. The table lists calls, subproblem size, per-call work and total work.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Recurrence relations. This is an exact toy work model on positive powers of two, not a benchmark or an exact merge-sort comparison count. Each non-leaf call makes two half-size calls and incurs its own size in additional work units. A size-one call costs one unit. Depth zero is the root; depth k contains the leaves. Bars aggregate work at a depth, not the number of calls. The table lists calls, subproblem size, per-call work and total work. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Count work within a level, then count the levels—including the base cases. Verify a proposed formula against both the recurrence and its boundary values.

title: Reductions
summary: A polynomial-time many-one reduction maps each instance of problem A to one instance of problem B, preserving yes and no answers. It lets an algorithm for B solve A after the translation. The mapping, its running time and both directions of the answer equivalence are separate proof obligations.
outcomes: Prove an instance mapping correct in both directions.
Use a reduction arrow correctly for algorithm reuse and hardness transfer.

sources.label: Cornell CS 2800: P, NP and reductions

labs.title: Complement the set, preserve the answer
labs.summary: An edge inside the independent set is exactly an edge missed by its complementary cover.
labs.equation: I independent ⇔ V\I is a vertex cover; (G,k) ↦ (G, |V|−k)
labs.assumptions: The fixed graph is the undirected five-cycle with edges AB, BC, CD, DE and EA. The mask chooses I using the displayed bit weights; every vertex not in I belongs to C. Dashed coral edges have both endpoints in I and no endpoint in C. The decision reduction asks for an independent set of size at least k versus a vertex cover of size at most |V|−k. The slider inspects certificates on one graph, while the edge argument below applies to arbitrary finite undirected graphs.

The mask chooses I using the displayed bit weights; every vertex not in I belongs to C. Dashed coral edges have both endpoints in I and no endpoint in C. The decision reduction asks for an independent set of size at least k versus a vertex cover of size at most |V|−k. The slider inspects certificates on one graph, while the edge argument below applies to arbitrary finite undirected graphs. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: For A≤pB, an efficient B solver transfers back to A; known hardness transfers forward from A to B. The arrow is a translator, not an algorithm that already solves either problem.

title: Regularization and penalties
summary: A penalty adds a stated preference to an optimization objective, such as smaller coefficients or sparse solutions. It changes the optimum rather than merely helping a solver reach the unpenalized answer. Whether that tradeoff improves prediction must be assessed separately from training fit.
outcomes: Derive the scalar L2 and L1 solution paths.
Separate regularized objectives, generalization evidence and decoupled weight decay.

sources.label: scikit-learn: linear models, penalties and robust regression
Dive into Deep Learning: weight decay
Loshchilov and Hutter: Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization

labs.title: Shrink smoothly—or switch a coefficient off
labs.summary: L2 turns the volume down; L1 can set this scalar coefficient exactly to zero.
labs.equation: minw ½(w−3)²+λw²/2 ⇒ w*=3/(1+λ); minw ½(w−3)²+λ|w| ⇒ w*=max(0,3−λ)
labs.assumptions: One dimensionless coefficient, fixed quadratic data-fit term and λ≥0. Curves show exact solution paths under two explicitly normalized penalties. The L1 soft-threshold formula uses the positive target 3; for general target z it is sign(z)max(|z|−λ,0). No validation dataset or optimizer trajectory is simulated.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Regularization and penalties. One dimensionless coefficient, fixed quadratic data-fit term and λ≥0. Curves show exact solution paths under two explicitly normalized penalties. The L1 soft-threshold formula uses the positive target 3; for general target z it is sign(z)max(|z|−λ,0). No validation dataset or optimizer trajectory is simulated. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Penalty geometry changes the solution: L2 shrinks continuously, whereas L1 has a threshold that can create exact zeros. The λ scale only makes sense alongside the loss and penalty normalization.

title: Rejection sampling
summary: Rejection sampling generates target draws by accepting or rejecting proposal draws with a probability derived from a valid envelope. If f(x)≤M g(x) everywhere on the target support, accepting x∼g with probability f(x)/(M g(x)) produces accepted draws with density f. A violated envelope invalidates that guarantee.
outcomes: Explain why accepted proposals follow the target density.
Separate envelope validity, theoretical efficiency and realized acceptance counts.

sources.label: Art Owen: non-uniform generation and acceptance-rejection

labs.title: Keep the points under the target curve
labs.summary: A valid roof preserves the target; an unnecessarily high roof wastes proposals.
labs.equation: f(x)=2x on [0,1], g(x)=1; M≥2; accept if U≤2x/M; P(accept)=1/M
labs.assumptions: The target is normalized, proposal x is uniform on [0,1], and U is an independent uniform draw. The chart places 80 fixed-seed proposal pairs at (x,MU), using seed 2718. Moving M reuses those pairs rather than drawing new ones. Dots under the target line are accepted; density and envelope lines are exact.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Rejection sampling. The target is normalized, proposal x is uniform on [0,1], and U is an independent uniform draw. The chart places 80 fixed-seed proposal pairs at (x,MU), using seed 2718. Moving M reuses those pairs rather than drawing new ones. Dots under the target line are accepted; density and envelope lines are exact. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Acceptance probability follows from the envelope ratio, not from visual similarity alone. A tighter valid envelope improves efficiency without changing the target law.

title: Sample spaces and events
summary: A probability model specifies a sample space Ω, a collection of measurable events, and a probability measure. Events are sets of outcomes; their probabilities come from the measure, not automatically from counting outcomes.
outcomes: Translate verbal events into set operations.
Distinguish disjointness, independence and equal likelihood.

sources.label: MIT 18.440: Probability and Random Variables — lecture notes

labs.title: Count the overlap only once
labs.summary: Union includes either event; intersection is the shared part.
labs.assumptions: A fair six-sided die has six equally likely elementary outcomes. A is the even faces and B is faces 1 through the selected threshold. Bars retain their original mass 1/6; unselected faces have no highlighted mass.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Sample spaces and events. A fair six-sided die has six equally likely elementary outcomes. A is the even faces and B is faces 1 through the selected threshold. Bars retain their original mass 1/6; unselected faces have no highlighted mass. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Counting favorable outcomes works only when the elementary outcomes being counted are equally likely.

title: Scalars, vectors, matrices, and tensors
summary: Scalars, vectors, and matrices have zero, one, and two indexed axes in array notation. Machine-learning libraries use tensor for a numerical array with any number of axes; axis meaning and shape determine valid operations.
outcomes: Distinguish shape, order, element count, and matrix rank.
Estimate payload memory while keeping axis semantics explicit.

sources.label: Deisenroth, Faisal, and Ong: Mathematics for Machine Learning

labs.title: Count the tensor slices
labs.summary: Name each axis before you multiply its sizes.
labs.equation: entries=∏ᵢ shapeᵢ; payload bytes=entries × bytes per entry
labs.assumptions: A contiguous float32 array has shape (batch,2,3). Each table is one 2×3 slice. Memory counts include only numerical payload, not object metadata, gradients, or copies.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Scalars, vectors, matrices, and tensors. A contiguous float32 array has shape (batch,2,3). Each table is one 2×3 slice. Memory counts include only numerical payload, not object metadata, gradients, or copies. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Array order counts axes; matrix rank counts independent columns. They are different meanings of rank, and neither is the number of entries.

title: Sets, relations, and functions
summary: Sets identify distinct elements; relations specify which ordered pairs belong together; functions impose an output rule on those pairs. Here a function A→B means a total function: every element of A has exactly one output in B. This contract is separate from whether outputs are shared or every codomain element is reached.
outcomes: Distinguish relations, partial functions, total functions and bijections.
Use explicit domain and codomain choices to reason about mappings.

sources.label: MIT Mathematics for Computer Science: relations and partial orders
MIT Mathematics for Computer Science: cardinality rules

labs.title: One arrow per input is a contract
labs.summary: Check the arrows leaving inputs before judging the arrows arriving at outputs.
labs.assumptions: A={a,b,c} and B={1,2,3} are fixed finite sets. Each arrow is one relation pair, and the tables enumerate the entire relation. The selector chooses four different relations, not stages of one algorithm. Partial functions are named explicitly; some sources use the unqualified word function for an at-most-one-output relation. Injective and surjective in the readout refer to total functions A→B under this lesson's convention.

Injective and surjective in the readout refer to total functions A→B under this lesson's convention. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Domain, codomain and the pair set are all part of the specification. A picture without those choices cannot establish totality or surjectivity.

title: Singular value decomposition
summary: Every real m×n matrix has an SVD A=UΣVᵀ. Orthogonal input and output directions reveal its nonnegative stretches, including for rectangular matrices that have no ordinary eigendecomposition.
outcomes: Interpret singular vectors and values for a rectangular map.
Check reduced-factor dimensions and reconstruction.

labs.title: From circle to ellipse
labs.summary: Follow a unit circle through a rectangular map and read its elliptical stretches.
labs.assumptions: The 3×2 example maps into the plane z=0. Reduced U has two orthonormal columns, Σ=diag(3,2), and Vᵀ=I. The plot shows only the first two output coordinates.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Singular value decomposition. The 3×2 example maps into the plane z=0. Reduced U has two orthonormal columns, Σ=diag(3,2), and Vᵀ=I. The plot shows only the first two output coordinates. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Singular values describe stretch magnitudes; input and output directions live in different spaces. Reduced U need not be square.

title: Sparse matrices
summary: Sparse formats store selected entries and their locations rather than allocating every cell. They save memory and computation only when the sparsity pattern, index overhead, and supported operations make that worthwhile.
outcomes: Calculate sparse-format storage overhead.
Choose a representation based on operations and structure.

labs.title: When does sparse storage win?
labs.summary: Zeros are free only after you pay for the address book.
labs.equation: CSR bytes = nnz·(value bytes + index bytes) + (rows+1)·pointer bytes
labs.assumptions: The toy matrix is 5×5. Values are float64 (8 bytes); column indices and row pointers are int32 (4 bytes). No object overhead, explicit zeros, or duplicate coordinates are included.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Sparse matrices. The toy matrix is 5×5. Values are float64 (8 bytes); column indices and row pointers are int32 (4 bytes). No object overhead, explicit zeros, or duplicate coordinates are included. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Sparse storage has a break-even density. Sparse computation also depends on access patterns, not just the percentage of zeros.

title: Split conformal prediction
summary: Split conformal prediction uses held-out calibration errors to turn a fixed predictor into a prediction set with a finite-sample marginal coverage guarantee under exchangeability.
outcomes: Compute the finite-sample corrected rank and prediction interval.
State the exchangeability assumption and distinguish marginal from conditional coverage.

sources.label: Angelopoulos and Bates: A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction
Authors' conformal prediction tutorial and notebooks

labs.title: Split conformal prediction: calculate and compare
labs.summary: Reserve errors you did not train on, rank them, then use the required rank as a prediction radius.
labs.assumptions: A predictor fixed before calibration; n=9 absolute residuals [0.2,0.3,0.4,0.5,0.7,0.9,1.1,1.4,2.0]. Calibration and future examples are exchangeable. Units are target units; the displayed new prediction is f(x)=5.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Split conformal prediction. A predictor fixed before calibration; n=9 absolute residuals [0.2,0.3,0.4,0.5,0.7,0.9,1.1,1.4,2.0]. Calibration and future examples are exchangeable. Units are target units; the displayed new prediction is f(x)=5. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: The corrected rank uses n+1, not n. The guarantee averages over exchangeable calibration and test examples; it is not a guarantee for every subgroup or every x.

title: Standard error
summary: The standard error of an estimator is the standard deviation of its sampling distribution. It measures variability of the estimator across repeated samples, not variability of individual observations. An estimated standard error is itself computed from data and depends on a valid sampling model.
outcomes: Distinguish standard deviation from standard error.
Explain the role of independence in the square-root sample-size rule.

sources.label: NIST: confidence limits and standard error of the mean

labs.title: Spread of data versus spread of estimates
labs.summary: More measurements stabilize the mean without making people or events identical.
labs.assumptions: Independent normal observations with fixed population mean and known population standard deviation σ=10. The exact mean distribution is normal. The σ/√n variance formula also holds for iid finite-variance observations without normality, but normal interval calibration need not then be exact.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Standard error. Independent normal observations with fixed population mean and known population standard deviation σ=10. The exact mean distribution is normal. The σ/√n variance formula also holds for iid finite-variance observations without normality, but normal interval calibration need not then be exact. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Label SD and SE explicitly: one describes the population spread, the other the uncertainty of an estimator under a sampling design.

title: Statistics
summary: Statistics uses observed data and a sampling model to estimate, compare or predict. The target matters: uncertainty about a population mean differs from uncertainty about one future observation. Valid uncertainty statements also depend on how observations were selected, whether they are independent and which assumptions justify the procedure.
outcomes: Distinguish estimation of a fixed mean from prediction of a future observation.
Explain why sample size affects confidence and prediction widths differently.

sources.label: NIST: confidence intervals and known-σ normal means
NIST: uncertainty in a single future response

labs.title: An average gets precise; the next observation still varies
labs.summary: More measurements sharpen the average, not the next measurement.
labs.equation: Mean CI: x̄±1.96σ/√n; future-observation PI: x̄±1.96σ√(1+1/n)
labs.assumptions: Independent observations from N(μ,σ²), unknown fixed μ and known σ=2. The future observation is independent and comes from the same population. The displayed sample mean is held at 3 while n varies to isolate interval widths. 1.96 rounds the standard-normal 97.5th percentile. Coverage is over repeated training samples, and also future observations for the prediction procedure; it is not a conditional coverage claim for every realized sample. No data are simulated.

The displayed sample mean is held at 3 while n varies to isolate interval widths. 1.96 rounds the standard-normal 97.5th percentile. Coverage is over repeated training samples, and also future observations for the prediction procedure; it is not a conditional coverage claim for every realized sample. No data are simulated. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Name the target before choosing an interval. Learning a mean more accurately does not remove individual variation, and more data cannot repair an invalid sampling model by itself.

title: Stochastic differential equations
summary: An SDE describes state evolution with both drift and stochastic forcing. In an Itô diffusion, Brownian increments scale with the square root of elapsed time. A solution is a random process: its mean, marginal spread and individual realizations answer different questions.
outcomes: Separate an SDE's mean, variance and a sample path.
Use Brownian scaling and distinguish exact grid transitions from numerical approximations.

sources.label: Higham: An Algorithmic Introduction to Numerical Simulation of SDEs
Art Owen: stochastic processes and simulation

labs.title: One noisy path is not the mean trajectory
labs.summary: The average can relax smoothly while every noisy realization keeps wandering.
labs.assumptions: A scalar Ornstein–Uhlenbeck Itô process with mean-reversion rate 1 per second and normalized state. Grid spacing is 0.05 seconds. The realization uses the exact Gaussian transition, not Euler–Maruyama, with Box–Muller normal draws from fixed pseudorandom seed 31415. The same innovations are reused across σ. Joining grid values does not reconstruct the continuous path between them.

Joining grid values does not reconstruct the continuous path between them. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Distinguish path randomness, distributional uncertainty and numerical time-step error. Here exact grid transitions remove discretization error at the grid points, not randomness or pseudorandom approximation.

title: Stochastic gradient descent
summary: SGD updates parameters using a sampled estimate of the objective gradient. Under uniform sampling of a finite mean loss, one example's gradient is unbiased conditional on the current parameters. Individual updates can still increase the full-data loss, and a fixed learning rate can leave persistent sampling noise.
outcomes: Derive an unbiased sample gradient for a finite mean objective.
Explain a constant-rate noise floor using exact mean and variance recurrences.
