Dive into Deep Learning: minibatch stochastic gradient descent

labs.title: The mean settles; one run keeps moving
labs.summary: A noisy compass can point correctly on average without tracing a straight route.
labs.assumptions: Loss for target z is ½(θ−z)², with targets {−1,1,3,5}, θ₀=0 and 30 updates. The moment curves assume fresh IID uniform sampling with replacement. The displayed path uses one disclosed fixed index sequence for reproducible comparison as η changes; its target sequence is in the numeric table. One-standard-deviation curves do not claim a coverage probability.

title: Student's t
summary: Student's t is a symmetric family with degrees of freedom ν>0 and heavier tails than a Gaussian. Standard t has mean zero only for ν>1 and finite variance ν/(ν−2) only for ν>2.
outcomes: Check which t moments exist.
Distinguish degrees of freedom, scale, and variance.

labs.title: Heavy tails approach a Gaussian
labs.summary: The central bell can look familiar while the tails behave differently.
labs.equation: T=Z/√(V/ν), Z~N(0,1), V~χ²ν independently; Var(T)=ν/(ν−2) for ν>2
labs.assumptions: The lab uses integer ν and unit scale. It compares t with a standard normal on [−6,6]; tails continue outside that window. Scale one does not mean variance one.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Student's t. The lab uses integer ν and unit scale. It compares t with a standard normal on [−6,6]; tails continue outside that window. Scale one does not mean variance one. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: At ν=1 this is the Cauchy law: symmetry does not rescue an undefined mean. As ν grows, standard t converges to standard normal.

title: Taylor approximation
summary: A Taylor polynomial matches a function's value and successive derivatives at an expansion point. Taylor's theorem adds a remainder under suitable smoothness assumptions. A finite polynomial is a local approximation; an infinite Taylor series represents its function only where the remainder tends to zero.
outcomes: Construct successive Maclaurin polynomials for exp(x).
Separate observed approximation error from a valid conservative bound.

sources.label: OpenStax: working with Taylor series and remainders

labs.title: Add one local term at a time
labs.summary: Matching the derivatives at one point is a promise about the neighborhood, not a blank cheque everywhere.
labs.assumptions: Maclaurin expansion of exp(x), plotted on [−2,2]. Dots compare the exact value and the polynomial at x=1. The uniform remainder bound uses exp(ξ)≤e² throughout this interval; it is intentionally conservative. These curves are not fitted to sampled data.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Taylor approximation. Maclaurin expansion of exp(x), plotted on [−2,2]. Dots compare the exact value and the polynomial at x=1. The uniform remainder bound uses exp(ξ)≤e² throughout this interval; it is intentionally conservative. These curves are not fitted to sampled data. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: State the expansion point, order and domain of use together with an error statement. A polynomial can match several derivatives perfectly at its center and still be inaccurate farther away.

title: Time and space complexity
summary: Complexity describes how an algorithm's resource requirements grow with a specified input size under a specified cost model. Time counts work; auxiliary space counts peak extra live storage. A mathematical recurrence defines an answer, but the evaluator chosen for it determines how much work is repeated.
outcomes: Explain why equivalent outputs can have different operation counts.
State complexity bounds with their input encoding, resource, case and cost model.

sources.label: Cornell CS 2110: complexity analysis and auxiliary space

labs.title: Same Fibonacci number, different computational bill
labs.summary: The answer is 55 either way. The bill can be nine additions or eighty-eight.
labs.assumptions: The naive evaluator returns n for n≤1, otherwise evaluates F(n−1) and F(n−2) recursively and adds them. The rolling evaluator initializes the pair (0,1), handles n≤1 directly, then adds once per index from 2 to n. Each sequence addition is one counted operation. The plot uses log₂(1+additions), not raw work or seconds, and shows integer inputs only. Memory is described in active frames and value slots, not measured bytes. The displayed small integers are exact; unbounded integer arithmetic requires a separate bit-cost analysis.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Time and space complexity. The naive evaluator returns n for n≤1, otherwise evaluates F(n−1) and F(n−2) recursively and adds them. The rolling evaluator initializes the pair (0,1), handles n≤1 directly, then adds once per index from 2 to n. Each sequence addition is one counted operation. The plot uses log₂(1+additions), not raw work or seconds, and shows integer inputs only. Memory is described in active frames and value slots, not measured bytes. The displayed small integers are exact; unbounded integer arithmetic requires a separate bit-cost analysis. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Compare algorithms for the same output, name the counted operation, and distinguish total work from peak storage. Log-scaled plots must not hide the raw counts.

title: Trace and determinant
summary: Trace is the sum of a square matrix's diagonal entries. Determinant is its signed volume-scaling factor. Both are invariant under a change of basis, but they summarize different properties of a transformation.
outcomes: Distinguish trace, signed volume, and invertibility.
Explain why a zero trace need not indicate lost dimensions.

labs.title: Stretch, flip, collapse
labs.summary: Add the stretches for trace; multiply them for signed volume.
labs.assumptions: The real 2×2 matrix A=diag(2,t) maps a unit square to a rectangle. Determinant carries orientation; geometric area is its absolute value.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Trace and determinant. The real 2×2 matrix A=diag(2,t) maps a unit square to a rectangle. Determinant carries orientation; geometric area is its absolute value. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Zero determinant collapses volume and means a square map is singular. Zero trace does not imply singularity.

title: Trees and directed acyclic graphs
summary: A finite undirected tree is connected and has no cycle; it has one simple path between each pair of vertices. A directed acyclic graph has no directed cycle, but may have shared descendants and cycles after arrow directions are forgotten. A rooted outward tree is a special DAG, not a synonym for every DAG.
outcomes: Distinguish undirected trees, rooted outward trees and general DAGs.
Trace dependency readiness and explain why topological orders can be nonunique.

labs.summary: A merge waits for every incoming dependency, not just the first parent to finish.
labs.assumptions: Six tasks A–F with edges A→B, A→C, B→D, C→D, D→E and D→F. An edge means its source must finish before its target. Each step immediately completes one ready task, choosing alphabetically among ties. No durations, worker limits, failures or asynchronous execution are modeled. The diagram retains original edges; the table counts prerequisites not yet emitted. A node marked done is an algorithm state, not an observed random variable.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Trees and directed acyclic graphs. Six tasks A–F with edges A→B, A→C, B→D, C→D, D→E and D→F. An edge means its source must finish before its target. Each step immediately completes one ready task, choosing alphabetically among ties. No durations, worker limits, failures or asynchronous execution are modeled. The diagram retains original edges; the table counts prerequisites not yet emitted. A node marked done is an algorithm state, not an observed random variable. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: A topological order respects every directed edge. It can be nonunique, and it does not by itself specify a parallel execution schedule.

title: Unconstrained and constrained optimization
summary: An unconstrained optimizer may move anywhere in its domain; a constrained optimizer must also satisfy a feasible set. At a boundary solution the objective gradient need not vanish: the constraint can block every improving direction that remains feasible.
outcomes: Calculate an active-bound optimum and its multiplier.
Explain why constrained stationarity differs from a zero objective gradient.

sources.label: Stanford EE364A: duality and optimality conditions

labs.title: The boundary changes the answer

title: Uniform
summary: A continuous uniform distribution assigns constant density across a finite interval. Equal-length subintervals have equal probability; individual points still have probability zero. Discrete uniform distributions instead assign equal masses to a finite set.
outcomes: Calculate uniform interval probabilities and moments.
Recognize the coordinate dependence of uniform sampling.

labs.takeaway: Uniformity depends on the coordinate system: a nonlinear transformation of a uniform variable is generally not uniform.

title: Variance and covariance
summary: Variance measures squared deviation from a mean. Covariance measures the expected product of centered variables and determines how uncertainty combines in sums. These finite-moment formulas assume finite second moments.
outcomes: Propagate variance with cross-covariance terms.
Check scaling, units and PSD constraints.

labs.takeaway: Variances add without a covariance term when variables are uncorrelated; independence is sufficient but not necessary.

title: Vector spaces, subspaces, span, basis, and dimension
summary: A vector space is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication over a chosen field. A span contains every linear combination of given vectors; a basis spans a space without redundant vectors, and its size is the dimension.
outcomes: Test a subspace and distinguish a span from a basis.
Recover coordinates in a specified basis and identify the space's dimension.

title: Approximate inference
summary: Approximate inference estimates a distribution or a quantity derived from it when exact computation is impractical. Sampling error and error from a restricted approximation family are distinct, and must be evaluated for the actual question being asked.
outcomes: Separate finite-sample uncertainty from error caused by a restrictive family.
Choose diagnostic queries that expose missing dependence instead of only checking marginal means.

labs.takeaway: More independent target samples reduce sampling error, but more computation of the same fixed approximation cannot remove its missing dependence.

title: Bayesian networks
summary: A Bayesian network combines a directed acyclic graph with one conditional probability distribution per node. Their product defines a normalized joint distribution. The graph expresses factorization assumptions; its arrows alone do not establish causal effects.
outcomes: Construct and query a joint distribution from local conditional tables.
Distinguish a graph's factorization assumptions from causal claims and inference complexity.

title: Belief propagation
summary: Belief propagation organizes inference as local messages summarizing information on either side of an edge. This lesson follows the schedule and information coverage of sum-product BP on a tree; the sum-product and max-product lessons develop the corresponding marginal and optimization calculations.

Distinguish a partial normalized belief from an exact tree marginal.

title: Conditional independence
summary: X and Y are conditionally independent given Z when their conditional joint distribution factorizes for each relevant value of Z. They may still be dependent after Z is hidden: averaging over a shared regime can couple otherwise independent observations.
outcomes: Verify conditional independence by factorizing a conditional joint table.
Explain why hidden shared regimes can produce dependence in pooled observations.

title: Conditional random fields

It combines input-dependent potentials and output compatibility, then normalizes over complete label structures. A linear chain supports efficient exact inference; a general output graph need not.

Explain why unary decisions, marginal decisions and joint decoding can disagree.

title: D-separation

outcomes: Apply the distinct blocking rules to chains, forks and colliders.
Explain why d-separation is a distribution-wide guarantee but d-connection only permits dependence.

title: Dynamic Bayesian networks

Distinguish compact transition factorization from independence of posterior state variables.

title: Exact inference
summary: Exact inference evaluates a specified probabilistic query without algorithmic approximation, subject to numerical precision and the model itself. Marginal probabilities, conditional probabilities and the most probable joint assignment are different queries; exact answers to one do not automatically solve another.
outcomes: Compute and distinguish marginal, conditional and joint-MAP queries.
Explain why combining marginal modes can differ from a most-probable joint assignment.

title: Expectation–maximization
summary: Expectation–maximization fits parameters in a latent-variable model by alternating posterior latent assignments under the current parameters with maximization of the expected complete-data log likelihood. Exact E and M steps do not decrease observed-data likelihood, but need not find a global maximum.
outcomes: Compute responsibilities and a weighted maximum-likelihood update.
Distinguish latent posterior inference, parameter fitting and a global-optimality guarantee.

title: Extended Kalman filter
summary: The extended Kalman filter uses local Jacobians to propagate covariance and form approximate corrections in nonlinear state-space models. It evaluates nonlinear functions at the current estimate but replaces their uncertainty propagation with a first-order approximation. The resulting Gaussian summary is generally not the exact nonlinear posterior.
outcomes: Derive a nonlinear sensor's EKF correction from its tangent.
Identify curvature and symmetry failures without mistaking approximate covariance for exact uncertainty.

title: Factor graphs

In a probabilistic model, nonnegative factors define a joint distribution after global normalization when the normalizer is finite and positive.
outcomes: Translate a factor product into a bipartite graph with correct scopes.
Distinguish factor weights, normalized probabilities and inference algorithms.

title: Forward-backward algorithm
summary: Forward–backward computes posterior state marginals in a finite-state HMM. Forward messages summarize evidence up to a time; backward messages summarize the remaining evidence conditional on that time's state. Their normalized product gives a smoothed marginal. This is different from filtering, which cannot use observations that have not yet arrived.
outcomes: Compute forward and backward messages with explicit conditioning.
Distinguish filtering, smoothing, observation likelihood and joint-path decoding.

title: Gibbs sampling
summary: Gibbs sampling repeatedly redraws a coordinate or block from its full conditional distribution while holding the other coordinates fixed. Each such update preserves the joint target. Strong dependence or disconnected conditional support can still prevent useful exploration; an update needing no rejection step is not a guarantee of fast mixing.
outcomes: Derive a Gibbs transition matrix from a small joint distribution.
Explain why target invariance and rejection-free updates do not certify fast mixing.

The graph propagates exact probability vectors for 40 single-coordinate updates and measures total variation to each curve's own target. It is not a random trajectory, an empirical convergence diagnostic or a count of complete sweeps.

labs.takeaway: Full conditional updates preserve the target without rejection, yet strong coupling can make transitions between high-probability regions rare.

title: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
summary: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo augments continuous parameters with momentum and uses gradients to propose moves through phase space. Numerical integration approximately preserves a Hamiltonian; a Metropolis correction accounts for integration error. Useful movement depends on geometry, step size and trajectory length, not acceptance probability alone.
outcomes: Calculate a leapfrog step and its Hamiltonian error.
Separate numerical accuracy, acceptance and movement through the target.

title: Hidden Markov models
summary: A hidden Markov model separates a latent state sequence from the observations it emits. In a first-order HMM, the next hidden state depends on the current hidden state, and each observation depends on its own state. Marginalizing the hidden sequence can produce temporal dependence in the observations; the observed process need not itself be first-order Markov.
outcomes: Factor a hidden-state sequence model into initial, transition and emission terms.
Explain why an observation histogram cannot describe all temporal dependence.

title: Junction-tree algorithm
summary: A junction tree reorganizes a graphical model into overlapping variable clusters arranged as a tree. Exact sum-product messages calibrate the clusters so their marginals agree on shared variables. This permits exact inference in cyclic models when the cluster tables remain computationally manageable.
outcomes: Compute separator messages and verify agreement between calibrated clusters.
Separate exactness conditions from the exponential cost of large clusters.

labs.summary: Make the computation a tree without pretending the original model was one.

labs.assumptions: Binary cycle A—B—C—D—A. Each original edge has weight 3 for equal states and 1 for unequal states. A has unary weight (1,a); all other unaries are 1. Assign φL=uA·ψAB·ψBC to cluster ABC and φR=ψCD·ψDA to cluster ACD, once each. Their separator is {A,C}. The fill edge AC adds no new factor. Both messages and calibrated cluster tables are computed by finite sums.

Both messages and calibrated cluster tables are computed by finite sums. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Exactness needs factor coverage and running intersection. Efficiency depends on cluster sizes, not just whether the original graph has a cycle.

title: Kalman filter
summary: The Kalman filter recursively predicts a state distribution and conditions it on a new measurement. With a Gaussian initial state, linear dynamics and observations, and the specified independent Gaussian noises, the filtering distribution remains Gaussian and its mean and covariance are exact. Incorrect noise or dynamics assumptions can still make the estimate unreliable.
outcomes: Compute a scalar prediction, innovation, gain and correction with units.
Separate exact conditional inference from the credibility of its modelling assumptions.

sources.label: Harvard: estimation, Kalman filtering and nonlinear filters
MathWorks: prediction and correction in estimation filters

labs.title: Let uncertainty decide how much to trust a reading
labs.summary: Trust is a ratio of uncertainties, not a fixed preference for the sensor.
labs.assumptions: One scalar predict–correct cycle. Previous position is N(1,1), with mean in metres and variance in m². Motion adds 1 m plus independent N(0,3) process noise, giving predicted N(2,4). The sensor observes z=x+v with independent v∼N(0,R), and reports z=5 m. Curves show the predicted prior, measurement likelihood as a function of x, and posterior; N(μ,P) uses variance as its second argument.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Kalman filter. One scalar predict–correct cycle. Previous position is N(1,1), with mean in metres and variance in m². Motion adds 1 m plus independent N(0,3) process noise, giving predicted N(2,4). The sensor observes z=x+v with independent v∼N(0,R), and reports z=5 m. Curves show the predicted prior, measurement likelihood as a function of x, and posterior; N(μ,P) uses variance as its second argument. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Prediction adds process uncertainty; correction combines prior and measurement precision. A smaller posterior covariance is meaningful only relative to a credible model.

title: Loopy belief propagation
summary: Loopy belief propagation iterates local BP updates on a graph with cycles. It can be useful, but convergence is not guaranteed and a stable fixed point need not give exact marginals. Update residuals measure numerical stabilization, not the error relative to the true distribution.
outcomes: Distinguish update convergence from agreement with exact marginals.
Specify and diagnose a loopy message-passing run without borrowing the tree exactness guarantee.

sources.label: Yedidia, Freeman & Weiss: free-energy approximations and generalized belief propagation
CMU 10-708: tree correctness and loopy belief propagation

labs.title: Stable messages, inaccurate beliefs
labs.summary: A stopped needle can still point to the wrong number.
labs.assumptions: Three spins sᵢ∈{−1,+1} form a triangle with coupling J=0.8 and field h=0.3. All six directed messages start at (0.5,0.5), are normalized after each synchronous update and use no damping. Symmetry keeps those messages equal, allowing one shared two-entry vector to represent them. Each outgoing update uses the one incoming message other than the recipient's; each node belief uses both incoming messages. Exact marginals enumerate all eight states.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Loopy belief propagation. Three spins sᵢ∈{−1,+1} form a triangle with coupling J=0.8 and field h=0.3. All six directed messages start at (0.5,0.5), are normalized after each synchronous update and use no damping. Symmetry keeps those messages equal, allowing one shared two-entry vector to represent them. Each outgoing update uses the one incoming message other than the recipient's; each node belief uses both incoming messages. Exact marginals enumerate all eight states. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Report both convergence diagnostics and evidence about accuracy. More iterations can remove update transients without removing the loop approximation error.

title: Markov chains
summary: A discrete-time Markov chain describes a state sequence whose next-state distribution, conditional on the current state, does not depend on earlier states.
outcomes: Propagate a distribution through a transition matrix.
Separate stationarity, uniqueness, and convergence instead of assuming they are equivalent.

labs.title: Markov chains: calculate and compare
labs.summary: Move probability mass along outgoing transitions, then add the arrivals.
labs.assumptions: Two states A and B; row distributions; a fixed transition matrix with nonnegative rows summing to 1. The initial distribution is π₀=(1,0).
labs.accessibilitySummary: Markov chains. Two states A and B; row distributions; a fixed transition matrix with nonnegative rows summing to 1. The initial distribution is π₀=(1,0). A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: The row vector after t transitions is π₀Pᵗ. For this irreducible, aperiodic chain it approaches (2/3,1/3).

title: Markov random fields
summary: A Markov random field describes an undirected dependency structure. A distribution factorized into nonnegative clique potentials, with a finite positive partition function, obeys the graph's separation-based conditional independencies. Its potentials score joint configurations rather than specify causal directions.
outcomes: Compute a partition function from nonnegative configuration weights.
Explain frustration and why unchanged one-variable marginals do not imply unchanged dependence.

labs.title: Three spins cannot all disagree
labs.summary: Local preferences can be impossible to satisfy simultaneously.
labs.assumptions: Three spins form a triangle, with one equal-strength pair potential exp(Jsᵢsⱼ) per edge and no external field. J is dimensionless. Two assignments have all spins equal; six have one spin different. The plotted probability is their exact normalized total, not a Monte Carlo estimate.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Markov random fields. Three spins form a triangle, with one equal-strength pair potential exp(Jsᵢsⱼ) per edge and no external field. J is dimensionless. Two assignments have all spins equal; six have one spin different. The plotted probability is their exact normalized total, not a Monte Carlo estimate. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Marginals can stay unchanged while interactions change radically. On this symmetric triangle every spin remains equally likely to be ±1, but joint agreement varies with J.

title: Max-product algorithm
summary: Max-product replaces summation with maximization in nonnegative-factor message passing to find a highest-weight joint assignment. On a tree, exact scores plus stored backpointers recover a joint MAP configuration. The resulting max scores are not marginal probabilities.
outcomes: Compute max messages and reconstruct one compatible joint MAP assignment.
Explain why normalized max scores do not equal posterior marginals.

sources.label: Stanford CS228: tree, sum-product and max-product message passing
Stanford CS228: variable elimination and inference queries

labs.title: Keep the best branch, then trace it back
labs.summary: A best score tells you how good; a backpointer tells you which choice.
labs.assumptions: Binary chain X—Y—Z with unaries X=(1,a), Y=(1,1), Z=(2,1) and pair factors [[3,1],[1,3]]. Root at Y. Store a maximizing source state for each recipient state, then choose the root and trace back. State 0 wins displayed ties; all globally maximizing assignments are also enumerated and listed. Exact sum-based marginals are a separate reference.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Max-product algorithm. Binary chain X—Y—Z with unaries X=(1,a), Y=(1,1), Z=(2,1) and pair factors [[3,1],[1,3]]. Root at Y. Store a maximizing source state for each recipient state, then choose the root and trace back. State 0 wins displayed ties; all globally maximizing assignments are also enumerated and listed. Exact sum-based marginals are a separate reference. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Use compatible backpointers to recover a joint assignment. Dividing max scores by their sum does not turn them into posterior marginals.

title: Metropolis-Hastings
summary: Metropolis–Hastings constructs a transition kernel that preserves a target distribution by correcting proposed moves with an acceptance probability. The correction depends on both target density and forward/reverse proposal probabilities. Preserving the target is not the same as having reached it from an arbitrary initial state.
outcomes: Calculate a corrected transition and verify detailed balance.
Distinguish proposal independence, proposal symmetry and independent output draws.

sources.label: Art Owen: Markov chain Monte Carlo and Gibbs sampling

labs.title: Correct the proposal, preserve the target
labs.summary: A proposal is an invitation, not a vote for the target distribution.
labs.assumptions: Three states have target masses π=(0.2,0.3,0.5). The independent proposal has q=(r,(1−r)/2,(1−r)/2), identical from every current state. All masses are positive. Bars compare exact invariant laws of the corrected and deliberately incorrect transition rules, not simulated histograms or convergence rates. Matrix rows are current states; columns are next states.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Metropolis-Hastings. Three states have target masses π=(0.2,0.3,0.5). The independent proposal has q=(r,(1−r)/2,(1−r)/2), identical from every current state. All masses are positive. Bars compare exact invariant laws of the corrected and deliberately incorrect transition rules, not simulated histograms or convergence rates. Matrix rows are current states; columns are next states. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: A state-independent proposal is not necessarily symmetric. The reverse/forward proposal ratio cancels only when those probabilities agree.

title: Particle filter
summary: A particle filter approximates the distribution of a hidden current state given observations so far. The bootstrap version proposes states from the transition model, weights them by the new observation likelihood and may resample. It is an online filtering application of Sequential Monte Carlo, not an exact inference guarantee.
outcomes: Trace a bootstrap particle filter with adaptive systematic resampling.
Distinguish weighted filtering error, ESS and surviving particle ancestry.

sources.label: Doucet & Johansen: particle filtering and smoothing tutorial
Elvira, Martino & Robert: Rethinking the Effective Sample Size

labs.title: Twenty moving hypotheses versus an exact filter
labs.summary: Move the hypotheses, score the sensor reading, then decide whether to copy survivors.
labs.assumptions: Five sites form a ring (4 neighbors 0). Transition probabilities are 0.6 to stay and 0.2 to either neighbor. A sensor reports the true site with probability 0.6, either adjacent site with 0.15 each and either remaining site with 0.05 each. The prior is uniform. Twenty prior-CDF-stratified particles start with four per site at t=1: assimilate the first reading directly, then propagate before each later reading. Observations are (0,1,1,3,4,4). Fixed pseudorandom seed 20260930 makes the run repeatable. Systematic resampling runs only when weight ESS is strictly below 10, resetting weights to 1/20. Plots show estimates before that resampling step, alongside an exact five-state filter.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Particle filter. Five sites form a ring (4 neighbors 0). Transition probabilities are 0.6 to stay and 0.2 to either neighbor. A sensor reports the true site with probability 0.6, either adjacent site with 0.15 each and either remaining site with 0.05 each. The prior is uniform. Twenty prior-CDF-stratified particles start with four per site at t=1: assimilate the first reading directly, then propagate before each later reading. Observations are (0,1,1,3,4,4). Fixed pseudorandom seed 20260930 makes the run repeatable. Systematic resampling runs only when weight ESS is strictly below 10, resetting weights to 1/20. Plots show estimates before that resampling step, alongside an exact five-state filter. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Separate sampling error, weight concentration and loss of ancestry. A particle count or ESS alone does not bound the error of a filtering query.

title: Probabilistic AI
summary: Probabilistic AI separates a model of uncertain quantities, a query about those quantities, an inference method and a decision rule. This section moves from graphical-model assumptions to exact and approximate inference, latent-variable learning and temporal state estimation. A numerical answer is meaningful only under its model and evidence assumptions.
outcomes: Separate representation, inference, learning and decision-making tasks.
Choose a relevant learning path and interpret a posterior without confusing it with an action.

sources.label: Berkeley CS188: decisions and expected utility
Doucet & Johansen: particle filtering and smoothing tutorial

labs.title: The belief stays fixed; the best action changes
labs.summary: Model → query → inference → decision: keep the four contracts separate.
labs.assumptions: Toy binary fault H has prior probability 0.1. P(+|fault)=0.8 and P(+|no fault)=0.2; one positive signal is observed. Intervening costs 1 only when there is no fault; waiting costs C only when there is a fault. Correct actions have zero loss. These abstract losses fully specify this simplified decision problem; there is no separate intervention cost or resource constraint. The slider changes C, never the probabilistic model or observation.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Probabilistic AI. Toy binary fault H has prior probability 0.1. P(+|fault)=0.8 and P(+|no fault)=0.2; one positive signal is observed. Intervening costs 1 only when there is no fault; waiting costs C only when there is a fault. Correct actions have zero loss. These abstract losses fully specify this simplified decision problem; there is no separate intervention cost or resource constraint. The slider changes C, never the probabilistic model or observation. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Probability describes belief under a model. A choice additionally depends on losses or utility. Changing those preferences should not silently change the posterior.

title: Sequential Monte Carlo
summary: Sequential Monte Carlo maintains weighted particles across a sequence of target distributions using importance weighting, resampling and suitable propagation or mutation. The sequence may follow real observations, as in particle filtering, or artificial intermediate targets for a static problem. This lab isolates one tempered weighting and resampling stage.
outcomes: Calculate a tempered importance update and systematic resampling choices.
Explain why uniform particle weights can coexist with lost support and approximation error.

sources.label: Del Moral, Doucet & Jasra: Sequential Monte Carlo samplers
Doucet & Johansen: particle filtering and smoothing tutorial
Elvira, Martino & Robert: Rethinking the Effective Sample Size

labs.title: Equal weights do not mean four different hypotheses
labs.summary: Four equal tickets can all point to only two places.
labs.assumptions: Four static hypotheses A,B,C,D have uniform prior and relative likelihood scores (1,2,4,16). Start with one equal-weight particle at each hypothesis. Each slider setting independently restarts a bridge from β=0 to the chosen β; it does not evolve the previous slider state. The exhaustive four-point starting population makes the pre-resampling weights exact for this toy target. Systematic resampling uses fixed offset 1/8 and thresholds (1/8,3/8,5/8,7/8), with no mutation. A randomized implementation draws its offset uniformly in [0,1/4).
labs.accessibilitySummary: Sequential Monte Carlo. Four static hypotheses A,B,C,D have uniform prior and relative likelihood scores (1,2,4,16). Start with one equal-weight particle at each hypothesis. Each slider setting independently restarts a bridge from β=0 to the chosen β; it does not evolve the previous slider state. The exhaustive four-point starting population makes the pre-resampling weights exact for this toy target. Systematic resampling uses fixed offset 1/8 and thresholds (1/8,3/8,5/8,7/8), with no mutation. A randomized implementation draws its offset uniformly in [0,1/4). A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Weight ESS measures concentration among particle weights, not the count of distinct states or correctness of their empirical distribution. Resampling can raise ESS while removing hypotheses.

title: Sum-product algorithm
summary: Sum-product computes marginal information by multiplying compatible factors and summing over unwanted states. On a factor tree, completed messages give exact marginals. On a cyclic factor graph, ordinary loopy updates lose that guarantee; exact inference may still be possible through elimination or junction-tree methods.
outcomes: Calculate a factor-to-variable message by summing compatible assignments.
Separate incoming messages, a local unary weight and the final normalized marginal.

sources.label: Stanford CS228: tree, sum-product and max-product message passing
CMU 10-708: tree correctness and loopy belief propagation

labs.title: A parity check sends a two-number message
labs.summary: The factor sums the possibilities you are not asking about.
labs.assumptions: Three independent binary unary distributions precede an even-parity constraint: P(X=1)=0.2, P(Y=1)=p and P(Z=1)=0.6. The factor is 1 when X⊕Y⊕Z=0 and 0 otherwise. The posterior is the independent unary model conditioned on satisfying parity. Only the central factor's scope is drawn; the three unary factors are shown in the table.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Sum-product algorithm. Three independent binary unary distributions precede an even-parity constraint: P(X=1)=0.2, P(Y=1)=p and P(Z=1)=0.6. The factor is 1 when X⊕Y⊕Z=0 and 0 otherwise. The posterior is the independent unary model conditioned on satisfying parity. Only the central factor's scope is drawn; the three unary factors are shown in the table. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: The outgoing factor message excludes the recipient's own unary information. Multiply that unary weight afterward, then normalize the belief.

title: Unscented Kalman filter
summary: The unscented Kalman filter approximates nonlinear moment propagation using deterministically selected sigma points and weights, then applies a mean/covariance correction. It does not require a Jacobian for this propagation. Sigma points are a numerical integration rule, not random posterior samples, and improved moment accuracy does not make a nonlinear posterior exactly Gaussian.
outcomes: Compute transformed moments from a specified sigma-point rule.
Distinguish exact moment agreement in a special example from exact nonlinear filtering.

sources.label: Harvard: estimation, Kalman filtering and nonlinear filters
MathWorks: extended and unscented filter algorithms

labs.title: Move a few weighted points through the curve
labs.summary: Move the points through the curve before averaging their outputs.
labs.equation: χ=(1,1+σ,1−σ); wᵐ=(0,½,½); wᶜ=(2,½,½); E[X²]=1+P; Var(X²)=4P+2P², P=σ²
labs.assumptions: One scalar measurement transform and correction. Prior X∼N(1,σ²); h(x)=x²; independent additive measurement-noise variance R=1; reading z=4. Scaled unscented-transform settings are dimension 1, α=1, κ=0 and β=2, giving λ=0. The three sigma points are deterministic. Mean and covariance weights differ. Exact moment agreement shown here is specific to this quadratic/Gaussian example and these weights.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Unscented Kalman filter. One scalar measurement transform and correction. Prior X∼N(1,σ²); h(x)=x²; independent additive measurement-noise variance R=1; reading z=4. Scaled unscented-transform settings are dimension 1, α=1, κ=0 and β=2, giving λ=0. The three sigma points are deterministic. Mean and covariance weights differ. Exact moment agreement shown here is specific to this quadratic/Gaussian example and these weights. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Sigma-point propagation can retain curvature terms missed by a tangent. Matching transformed moments still leaves a Gaussian conditioning approximation.

title: Variable elimination
summary: Variable elimination computes a marginal by repeatedly multiplying the factors containing a hidden variable and summing that variable out. Distributivity preserves the answer, but elimination order controls the scope and size of intermediate factors.
outcomes: Carry out bucket multiplication and summation with explicit scopes.
Compare elimination orders without confusing computational cost with changes to the query result.

sources.label: Stanford CS228: factor trees and message passing

labs.title: The answer stays; the intermediate table grows
labs.summary: Remove the leaves first, or pay to connect them through a giant table.
labs.assumptions: Binary variables form a star centered at H with leaves A,B,C,Q. Every H–leaf factor is [[3,1],[1,3]]. Unary weights are H=(1,1), A=(1,2), B=(2,1), C=(1,3); Q has no unary preference. Retain Q and eliminate the other four variables. Table counts refer to dense bucket products before summing and dense output factors after summing, not timing measurements.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Variable elimination. Binary variables form a star centered at H with leaves A,B,C,Q. Every H–leaf factor is [[3,1],[1,3]]. Unary weights are H=(1,1), A=(1,2), B=(2,1), C=(1,3); Q has no unary preference. Retain Q and eliminate the other four variables. Table counts refer to dense bucket products before summing and dense output factors after summing, not timing measurements. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: A good order changes computational cost, not the mathematical marginal. Factor scope and cardinality determine the expensive intermediates.

title: Variational inference
summary: Variational inference turns distribution approximation into optimization over a chosen family. In the common KL(q||p) formulation, maximizing an evidence lower bound avoids evaluating an intractable normalizing constant, but cannot remove limitations of the family.
outcomes: Derive the ELBO identity from an unnormalized target.
Explain how family restrictions and divergence direction change approximation behavior.

sources.label: Blei, Kucukelbir & McAuliffe: Variational Inference — A Review

labs.title: One family, two tempting modes
labs.summary: The best fit inside a narrow family can prefer one explanation over a balanced view of both.
labs.assumptions: Unnormalized weights w=(49,1,1,49) have Z=100. The restricted family ties both independent Bernoulli marginals to a: q=((1−a)²,a(1−a),a(1−a),a²). Logs are natural. The slider evaluates an objective; it does not run an optimizer. Here log Z is a generic log normalizer, not a data evidence unless w is specified as a joint data–latent density.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Variational inference. Unnormalized weights w=(49,1,1,49) have Z=100. The restricted family ties both independent Bernoulli marginals to a: q=((1−a)²,a(1−a),a(1−a),a²). Logs are natural. The slider evaluates an objective; it does not run an optimizer. Here log Z is a generic log normalizer, not a data evidence unless w is specified as a joint data–latent density. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Lower KL(q||p) can improve agreement probability while worsening marginal means. The chosen objective and family determine which compromises are attractive.

title: Viterbi decoding
summary: Viterbi decoding uses dynamic programming to find a most probable complete hidden-state path for fixed HMM parameters and observations. It keeps the best prefix ending in each state, then traces predecessor choices backward. Maximizing a whole-path probability is a different decision problem from maximizing each posterior state marginal separately.
outcomes: Recover a joint MAP sequence using max scores and backpointers.
Explain a concrete disagreement between joint-path decoding and marginal decisions.

sources.label: Jurafsky and Martin: Hidden Markov Models
Stanford CS228: sum and max inference by elimination

labs.title: The best whole path is not four separate decisions
labs.summary: Choose a coherent route through the sequence, not a winner in every column.
labs.equation: δ₁(j)=log π(j)+log B(j,y₁); δₜ(j)=log B(j,yₜ)+maxᵢ[δₜ₋₁(i)+log A(i,j)]
labs.assumptions: Observed string 1100, uniform initial state probabilities, hidden persistence 0.8. The control changes the probability that an observation matches its state. Viterbi uses log scores and backpointers; smoothing uses sums over paths. Ties within 1e−12 in log score prefer the lower predecessor or final-state index. Binary path labels and marginal probabilities share the vertical scale but are explicitly different quantities; connecting lines do not interpolate hidden states.
labs.accessibilitySummary: Viterbi decoding. Observed string 1100, uniform initial state probabilities, hidden persistence 0.8. The control changes the probability that an observation matches its state. Viterbi uses log scores and backpointers; smoothing uses sums over paths. Ties within 1e−12 in log score prefer the lower predecessor or final-state index. Binary path labels and marginal probabilities share the vertical scale but are explicitly different quantities; connecting lines do not interpolate hidden states. A data table and numeric summary accompany the graph.
labs.takeaway: Joint MAP minimizes whole-sequence zero–one loss. Independent marginal decisions minimize the expected number of state-label errors; neither objective universally dominates the other.
